💡 Key Takeaways

  • Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

According to recent reports, when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in newly introduced ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Industry observers note that over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

Sources indicate that the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Recent findings suggest that thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Sources indicate that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

From Callback to Confidence: How Engineering an ESS for Field Reduces the Costly Callbacks

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (279 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Installer on-site callbacks are the silent margin killer in residential energy management and storage.
  • Industry observers note that preventing callbacks is not only the installer’s responsibility.
  • This paper walks through the anatomy of a callback, the hidden cost stack it creates, the actual root causes industry-wide and in our own data, and the engineering, support, and service decisions made to reduce callback risk before the truck rolls, and to absorb the cost when it can’t be avoided.

Installer on-site callbacks are the silent margin killer in residential energy management and storage. They consume labor, fuel, new project scheduling capacity, and homeowner trust in ways that rarely show up in the original bid. Across the industry, callbacks come from three sources that often overlap: system designs that are too complex to cleanly install, hardware failures after the system is in service, and challenges that arise in the field during installations. Most contractors only feel the cumulative cost years after an install have rolled past. Conversely highly reliable system hardware allows a contractor to confidently “right-size” the project price bid, helping to bring in more business in a period of industry transition.

Industry observers note that preventing callbacks is not only the installer’s responsibility. How the system is engineered, built, and supported all impact callbacks. FranklinWH has focused on quality products and the simplest install, with hardware held to an independently verified reliability standard. The company provides support before, during and after the installation. All of this helps to minimize callbacks. Service data indicates once system complexity and hardware failure are engineered down, the dominant driver of post-install activity that remains is the installation stage itself, the real-world variability of the field. That, too, is a problem to solve at the source, not one to pass to the installer.

This paper walks through the anatomy of a callback, the hidden cost stack it creates, the actual root causes industry-wide and in our own data, and the engineering, support, and service decisions made to reduce callback risk before the truck rolls, and to absorb the cost when it can’t be avoided.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sylvester Stallone has been a Hollywood institution for so long — his breakthrough movie Rocky premiered 50 years ago — that his previous underdog status as a struggling actor seems perfectly mythic in the new behind-the-scenes biographical drama I Play Rocky.

The fairy-tale aspect of I Play Rocky comes from its background story. In this, young Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) is a virtually homeless outsider, working at a movie theater, who after spending 16 months on writing eight screenplays, joins the creative zeitgeist of 1970s Hollywood, also known as the American Renaissance. It is this personal journey that illuminates the Stallone legend that climaxes with Rocky winning the Academy Award for best picture over such esteemed movies as Taxi Driver, Network, Bound for Glory, and All the President’s Men.

Starting with Stallone practicing elocution (using Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric”) to soften his rough Latest York accent, the film then places him against odds in an era of cultural ferment that included such films as Altman’s The Long Goodbye and Coppola’s The Conversation. (Stallone pays particular attention to the intonation of Coppola’s actors repeating the line “He’d kill us if he found out.”) Screenwriter Peter Gamble doesn’t make that detail ominous but simplifies the life-or-death aspect of Stallone’s career and artistic ambition as part of the wannabe actor’s desperate, working-class consciousness — inspired by viewing the heavyweight championship boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner. It’s easier to take than the sociological theme in Green Book, the egregious previous film of director Peter Farrelly. I Play Rocky regains the genial humanism of such Farrelly brothers’ movies as Me, Myself and Irene, Stuck on You, and The Ringer, and especially the Farrelly brothers’ script for Outside Providence.

Kiki Seto (Talia Shire) and Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky.

Stallone’s ambition is epitomized by his insistence that the Rocky screenplay he wrote in four days and sold to producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff can be filmed only starring himself. He demands, “I play Rocky.” That’s not a playground taunt in the milieu of financial bargaining and egotism that’s gleefully depicted by a series of Hollywood types — P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as Winkler and Chartoff, Rob Demery as Joe Frazier, and a standout cameo by Trevor St. John as a self-serious fight coordinator.

Recent findings suggest that in Hollywood’s gladiatorial circus, Stallone’s striving and eventual success become a credible moral victory. He must claim his own identity and career path separately from his worldly father Frank (Matt Dillon gives a moving characterization of a parent’s cynicism, affection, and personal regret). His wife Sasha (AnnaSophie Robb) encourages him: “I’d rather be optimistic and be wrong than pessimistic and be right.” These backstage details (including a hostile producer who dismisses Stallone as “a droopy-eyed hack actor”) make I Play Rocky a credible and appealing saga of Stallone’s indefatigable confidence. The movie rejects the sort of dark, objectionable narcissism that we saw in the Springsteen hagiography Deliver Me from Nowhere.

It is important that the filmmakers accurately measure Rocky’s significance. Farrelly and Gamble mix film history with good sense and humor when portraying wild-eyed director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) deep in his own world of pragmatic professionalism (“Great art never comes through compromise”). They also capture Stallone’s own, uncanny sense of achieving the proper effect — not so much when Rocky emotes to his manager Mickey as when, in a startling shot, he points to details in a significant-screen image of Kirk Douglas in Champion, from 1948.

Putting Rocky in proper perspective is a curatorial feat. It recognizes Stallone’s film as a work of pop lore. Its popularity gave Hollywood the opportunity to ignore scary powerful art like Scorsese’s Taxi Driver in favor of the folk and commercial elements that are easily enjoyed in American culture — although missing from Millennial film culture. Remember: In 1976, Rocky seemed an artificial retread of old boxing films, pilfering the ethnic sentimentality of Marty, On the Waterfront, and Requiem for a Heavyweight as if Muhammad Ali had never happened.

But I Play Rocky works differently. It recalls Stallone’s response to Wepner (“This guy won’t go down!”) to achieve the authentic Millennial pop lore of Better Man, Song Sung Blue, Back 2 America, Power Ballad, and the upcoming Madden. (These restorative myths correct the disappointing Creed sequels that failed to live up to Rocky.) I Play Rocky channels Stallone’s personal perseverance to enlighten our current demoralized sensibilities.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of Fresh Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, but California Rep.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

According to recent reports, but California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he remarked.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very glitch that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she noted. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

Sources indicate that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

It has been revealed that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

Industry observers note that amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

Industry observers note that BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

Sources indicate that the next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

The impulse to reverse course on Trump’s alliance policy is understandable. The president has brought two years of vitriol and abuse upon the United States’ closest friends—from a trade war with Canada to threats to invade Greenland—with clear strategic costs. But the flaws of his approach, and its broad unpopularity with the American public, are not a mandate for reflexive reversal. Nevertheless, there is a growing view in both Washington and allied capitals that, under upcoming congressional leadership and with a new administration just two years away, Washington should take a maximally conciliatory approach to its friends. Apology tours, day-one tariff repeals, and the reinstatement of withdrawn troops in allied countries are all cited as necessary steps to regain lost trust.

Recent findings suggest that the problem with that approach is twofold. First, it prioritizes rebuilding trust with allies over something more important—transforming old alliance bargains. The U.S. alliance system was built for the early Cold War world and used conventional and nuclear deterrence to keep threats far from the country’s shores. Its record of success is remarkable: No U.S. ally has ever been attacked, and U.S. treaty guarantees were invoked just once—on Washington’s behalf following the Sept. 11 attacks. But in the post-Cold War world, the United States and its allies need to cooperate on artificial intelligence, securing vital supply chains, aligning on climate and industrial policy, and combatting threats in cyberspace. Reembracing alliances without insisting on much-needed modernization would miss the chance to update them for new opportunities and threats, leaving the U.S. alliance network far less effective.

In a recent development, reflexive policy reversal also ignores the ways in which allies approach the United States differently after Trump’s reelection and punitive second term. U.S. leadership on global challenges is now constrained by a four-year problem. Having seen the United States succumb to political chaos twice in a decade at the expense of its own global position, friends and partners around the world will assume that any future deal they cut with the United States is only good for four years, until power changes hands again. If the United States wants close cooperation from allies in this world, then it will have to give them some space to build autonomy and resilience in case Washington defects again.

Taking this advice would prompt Democratic leaders to resist conventional wisdom on two complications in particular: tariffs and defense burden-sharing.

Trump’s trade war has proven to be both bad policy and bad politics, and it has hit U.S. allies as hard as its competitors. Many allies will argue that tariff reversals are an essential precondition for earning back their trust in the post-Trump era. But pursuing a unilateral, blanket repeal of tariffs on allies and partners—whether as an act of Congress or in the early days of a new administration—would be a mistake. Instead, Democrats can use their newfound control of Congress to check illegal tariffs that have driven up costs for American consumers, such as tariffs on forced labor, and repeal senseless duties on Canada. Such steps should pave the way for a broader international-economic agenda in 2029 that strengthens the U.S. economy and restores predictability for workers and businesses. That could start with prepares to lower remaining tariffs on allies as part of a new economic bargain that includes bold, joint action against unfair Chinese trade practices and new agreements on technology and supply chain cooperation. Trump’s wanton tariff leverage should be parlayed into new cooperation, rather than freely ceded, to serve the bottom line of the American people and those in friendly nations.

A phased initiative for tariffs also points the way for Democrats to take a new approach to allied burden-sharing on security and defense. Denouncing Trump’s abusive approach, elevating alliances as a strategic priority, and unambiguously acknowledging China and Russia as shared threats can begin to improve U.S. relationships. But congressional Democrats should not launch an apology tour or provide slavish reassurances that undercut the progress that allies have made toward better defending themselves. Instead, Democrats should encourage allies to continue investing in their own defense in Europe and Asia, and adjust U.S. policies to actively support these efforts, even if the United States loses some influence as allies take on a greater role. Following a disastrous war with Iran that has cratered U.S. defense stockpiles, Congress should fund super-charged efforts to coproduce munitions and other critical systems alongside allies to rebuild deterrence. And, notwithstanding the flawed process by which the Trump administration has approached its ongoing global force posture review, Democrats should bring an open mind to the strategic benefits of a rebalanced U.S. presence in some regions.

In a recent development, newly empowered, Democrats should seize the opportunity to reassert allies as central to U.S. global strategy. But that should not mean a return to old patterns of burden-sharing, which too often let allies off the hook and created dependencies that they will no longer accept and the United States should not encourage. Nor should Washington fall back on traditional modes of collaboration, which privileged military commitments whose benefits may feel abstract and undervalued the economic and technological domains that most benefit Americans. The Trump shock to the U.S. alliance system has come with high costs, and most of this approach should be rejected. But Democrats should also identify where policies of the past two years have created fresh openings or new leverage and use those opportunities wisely, rather than giving them away for free. Rebuilding critical U.S. relationships is essential, but it is a long-term project. After two Trump presidencies, quick policy concessions will not overcome the structural sources of allied skepticism about U.S. reliability.

The world that the next U.S. president meets in 2029 will look dramatically different than the one of 2025 or 2021. The post-Cold War era has ended in a convulsion, and the Trump presidency, which has intentionally ravaged the United States’ global role, has two years of chaos remaining. Rather than attempt to run down the clock through 2028 and overturn his disastrous policies wholesale, congressional Democrats have a chance to build a policy bridge to a new era. By prioritizing the renovation and resilience in the U.S. global alliance system, Congress can work with—rather than in reflexive opposition to—the epochal global shifts that have taken place and position Washington to inaugurate a new era of global leadership in 2029.

Sources indicate that rebecca Lissner is a senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as a deputy assistant to the president and principal deputy national security advisor to the vice president in the Biden-Harris administration. X: @RebeccaLissner.

#30403. How Xi Sees a Weakened Trump

How Xi Sees a Weakened Trump

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that voters dealt U.S.
  • According to recent reports, I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump.
  • President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Sources indicate that voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

According to recent reports, I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the fresh framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

Voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

Industry observers note that I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the new framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

This matters because both Xi and Trump place considerable importance on personal diplomacy between heads of state. Trump visited China in May, and Xi traveled to the United States in September. During those meetings, according to the Chinese readout, they agreed to establish a newly introduced framework for bilateral relations: a “constructive and strategically stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” Xi also called for a relationship characterized by “cooperation as the priority, managed competition, controlled differences, and the prospect of peace.”.

Trump, for his part, repeatedly emphasized his good personal relationship with Xi and expressed confidence that U.S.-China relations could succeed under their leadership.

According to recent reports, despite their very different political backgrounds and governing philosophies, Xi and Trump, who have both sought to expand their own authority at home, share a belief that strong leaders can play a decisive role in national decision-making. Beijing routinely emphasizes the strategic importance of diplomacy conducted by heads of state. Trump, meanwhile, distrusts the traditional foreign-policy bureaucracy and prefers to negotiate deals directly with other leaders. Both seem to believe that once leaders reach an understanding, many complicated problems between their countries can be resolved.

But there is a fundamental difference between them. Xi’s autocratic status allows him to translate his personal diplomatic preferences into Chinese government policy. Trump, despite his unusually personal approach to presidential decision-making, cannot entirely circumvent Congress, the judiciary, or other domestic political forces—especially after the recent midterm results.

According to recent reports, that difference was less visible when Republicans controlled both the White House and Congress. After returning to office, Trump enjoyed considerable authority within the Republican Party, while a supine Congress offered little effective resistance to his policies, even when pro-Ukrainian Republicans objected to his attempts to cozy up to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi had reason to believe that maintaining a stable personal relationship with Trump could help stabilize Washington’s China policy and perhaps even facilitate adjustments to U.S. positions on sensitive challenges through direct negotiations between the two leaders.

In a recent development, the midterms have changed that. With Democrats controlling Congress, Trump retains substantial authority over foreign affairs, but major agreements he reaches with Xi will face greater congressional scrutiny and potential challenges. On Taiwan and advanced technology in particular, especially after the Jensen Huang scandal, Democrats are not necessarily more accommodating toward China than Republicans. If Trump attempts to make significant concessions to Beijing in these areas, Democrats could use hearings, investigations, budgetary powers, and legislation to obstruct him—and turn any such concessions into political ammunition.

Industry observers note that for Trump, however, the more difficult constraint may come from his own party’s political interests. He cannot run for president again, however much he wants to, but Republicans must defend the White House and seek to regain Congress in 2028. If Democrats portray a Trump-Xi agreement as sacrificing Taiwan’s security or undermining America’s technological advantage, Republican candidates will face an uncomfortable choice. Supporting Trump could expose them to accusations of being soft on China; opposing him could alienate MAGA voters. Trump may be willing to disregard Democratic criticism, but he cannot entirely ignore his party’s electoral prospects or his own political legacy.

It has been revealed that this creates a paradox. Having lost his congressional majority, Trump may have a stronger incentive to demonstrate his leadership through foreign-policy achievements, making him more eager to reach a major agreement with Xi. Yet the greater his need to present such an agreement as a victory for the United States, the less room he has to appear to be making concessions to China. His weakened political position increases his incentive to strike a deal while simultaneously narrowing the concessions he can offer.

Xi is likely to recognize this. Rather than downgrading the importance of his personal relationship with Trump, he may become even more determined to preserve that direct channel of communication. Compared with Democratic politicians, Trump remains more inclined to approach U.S.-China relations transactionally and more willing to adjust specific policies according to his own judgment. From Chinese leaders’ perspective, he remains someone they can deal with—but they may no longer trust his ability to deliver. He remains a president worth negotiating with.

According to recent reports, beijing set the language after the Trump-Xi meeting in September, with little pushback from the White House. From Beijing’s perspective, the framework represents more than an effort to move beyond the intense trade confrontation of recent years. It also signals, in China’s interpretation, that Washington is beginning to accept China as an equal strategic power and is willing to keep bilateral competition within certain limits. Beijing clearly hopes that the principles of “respect” and “strategic stability” will extend to issues it considers central to its interests, particularly Taiwan and technology.

Yet Trump’s acceptance of this diplomatic language does not mean the entire U.S. political system is on board. Trump himself may well not understand the implications of the Chinese language. For Washington, strategic stability is more about managing conflict, protecting U.S. interests, and preserving competitive advantages.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry’s response to the results of the U.S. midterms offers an indication of Beijing’s approach. Rather than commenting on Trump’s political defeat, its spokesperson emphasized China’s willingness to continue implementing the understandings reached by the two presidents and to advance their constructive, strategically stable relationship.

Xi is unlikely to repudiate diplomatic achievements in which he has invested substantial political capital simply because of a U.S. midterm election. On the contrary, he has good reason to reaffirm the framework and invoke it when pressing Washington to honor the understandings reached between the two leaders.

According to recent reports, but I suspect that the more Beijing emphasizes the framework in its diplomatic rhetoric, the more cautious it will become in practice. This brings us to a second question: How does Xi interpret U.S. politics itself?

Industry observers note that when Trump won reelection in 2024, Republicans also captured both chambers of Congress, and the media was eager to trumpet a latest era of dominant Trumpism. Just two years later, Democrats have won their biggest victory in generations. This sharp reversal may reinforce Xi’s perception that U.S. politics lacks stability and continuity.

In a recent development, yet Xi would be making a mistake if he interpreted U.S. political divisions as evidence that China now enjoys a greater strategic opportunity. In U.S. politics, the two parties may fight bitterly over domestic problems and presidential authority while maintaining considerable agreement on strategic competition with China.

It has been revealed that I expect Beijing to gradually shift the emphasis of its U.S. policy over the next two years. It will continue to maintain Xi’s personal relationship with Trump, seek to implement existing agreements, and avoid another serious confrontation over trade or security. At the same time, it will lower its expectations that leader-to-leader diplomacy can fundamentally redirect U.S.-China relations. Instead, Beijing will accelerate attempts to reduce China’s vulnerability to shifts in U.S. policy during a prolonged period of strategic competition.

In a recent development, such an adjustment would not mean Xi is preparing for an all-out confrontation with the United States. Because Beijing increasingly recognizes that the competition will be prolonged, it has greater reason to avoid a direct clash before the conditions are in its failure. Maintaining basic stability in U.S.-China relations remains a way to buy time for China’s own development.

The new framework established by Xi and Trump this year is therefore unlikely to be abandoned easily. Beijing still needs it, and so does Trump. But their expectations may increasingly diverge. Xi wants the framework to provide China with long-term strategic stability, while Trump is more likely to see it as a means of managing relations with Beijing and securing diplomatic achievements during the remainder of his presidency.

For Xi, the central lesson of the midterms may be that he can build personal trust with Trump but he cannot entrust the future of U.S.-China relations to Trump alone.

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Residential solar is finding a new place to call home: the backyard.

Outer Spaces, a new organization founded by the entrepreneurs behind outdoor living brand Outer, is introducing a solar-powered pavilion that combines photovoltaic generation, battery storage and usable outdoor living space. The company’s first product, OS1, can be designed for multiple functions, including an outdoor kitchen, office, gym or gathering space, while generating electricity and providing backup power for the home.

Outer Spaces is planning to produce outdoor structures that integrate solar PV and energy storage. Credit: Outer Spaces.

The California-based company is positioning OS1 as a fresh category of residential energy infrastructure that goes beyond conventional rooftop arrays and garage-mounted batteries. It builds on the growing interest in solar structures that also serve a secondary purpose.

In a recent development, OS1 combines a solar pavilion with a finished outdoor power deck. Solar panels integrated into the overhead structure generate electricity, while a thin battery storage system is housed beneath the deck. According to Outer Spaces, the combination allows the structure to produce energy throughout the day and provide backup power during outages.

Rather than competing exclusively with traditional rooftop solar, OS1 offers homeowners an additional way to use available property for energy production, particularly when roof aesthetics, space limitations, or homeowner preferences become obstacles to conventional installations.

Industry observers note that outer Spaces describes OS1 as a modular system designed for rapid on-site assembly, with minimal to no excavation required. The manufacturer indicates installation avoids traditional construction steps such as concrete pouring and lumber cutting. Once the structure is assembled, a licensed electrician then connects its energy system to the customer’s home.

The product’s first availability is scheduled for 2027, beginning in Southern California and select additional markets; pricing is expected to be declared in early 2027.

Solar canopies and pergolas have increasingly incorporated features such as EV charging, lighting, fans and weather protection, giving homeowners additional reasons to invest in solar outside the traditional rooftop model.

In a recent development, outer Spaces represents another potential avenue for expanding residential solar adoption through design-driven products. The opportunity will ultimately depend on pricing, installation economics, permitting requirements and the system’s measurable energy performance.

Sources indicate that outer Spaces plans to showcase OS1 publicly for the first time at RE+ 2026, Nov. 16 to 19, in Las Vegas.

Japan’s Defense Lessons From Ukraine and the Middle East

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms.
  • Recent findings suggest that since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Industry observers note that since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

In a recent development, expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Recent findings suggest that since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

According to recent reports, expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

According to recent reports, japan’s focus on production capacity reflects a change in the way that military planners think about deterrence. Russia’s yearslong war against Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated the prolonged, high-intensity, resource-draining nature of modern warfare. Some analysts now expect a potential conflict over Taiwan to play out in similar ways, rather than the quick, decisive campaign that many experts had long assumed as their base case.

In a recent development, NATO frames deterrence around three elements: capability (does a state have the weapons to defend itself?), credibility (would it actually use them?), and communication (does the adversary understand what it would be up against?). In a long, high-intensity conflict, each of these three pillars is increasingly shaped by production capacity.

According to recent reports, production capacity affects the availability of the weapons needed for military operations both in preparation during peacetime and during an ongoing war. Recent conflicts have underlined two aspects of replenishment capability: the replacement rate (whether weapons output keeps pace with consumption in the battlespace) and the cost-to-kill ratio (how much a defensive weapon costs compared to the offensive threat that it counters).

In terms of credibility, a longer conflict is not just about the willingness to use force but also the willingness to sustain it for the duration of the conflict. The durability of public and private investment signals whether a state can support production throughout a prolonged conflict.

In terms of communication, an adversary’s calculation—and hence the deterrent effect—is affected by the signal sent by investing political and financial capital in defense production capacity.

In a recent development, viewed through this framework, recent announcements by the Japanese government and reports on the forthcoming reforms show how production capacity relates to the three pillars of deterrence. To upgrade capability, Tokyo has indicated that it will accelerate support for domestic industry. To this end, the Japanese government is planning to release a newly introduced defense industrial base strategy, likely to include new subsidies to support defense firms’ production capacity. One proposal is to extend an existing scheme to the acquisition and maintenance of production facilities for ammunition and other critical supplies necessary for sustained combat capability. Through greater governmental support, Tokyo aims to establish spare defense production capacity that could sustain protracted and high-intensity warfare.

Industry observers note that to enhance credibility—by demonstrating willingness not just to spend now but also to keep spending in the future—Tokyo is working to bolster the domestic defense investment landscape. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has urged Japanese financial institutions to provide investment and loans to grow the domestic defense sector, and lenders are responding.

In May, the Development Bank of Japan, a state-owned institution, eased its restrictions on financing domestic arms manufacturers. Private banks are also increasing their involvement in the sector. MUFG Bank, one of Japan’s largest private-sector banks, is reportedly planning to establish criteria for lending to defense-related companies after having previously been cautious. These measures normalize defense-related investments in peacetime, but they do not guarantee the financial sector’s commitment to invest in case of a longer conflict.

In a recent development, in April, the Defense Ministry stated that Japan must not allow an adversary to believe that prolonging a conflict would ensure the success of an invasion, emphasizing the importance of stockpiling and domestic production. Koizumi has made the connection between defense production and deterrence increasingly explicit. Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa has also been explicit about investing in the industrial base for dual-use goods in order to strengthen Japan’s ability to sustain military operations.

In terms of communicating deterrence, Tokyo is matching these efforts with political signaling that its new defense-industrial posture is a long-term change that’s here to stay.

In a recent development, there are still two major gaps in Japan’s production planning for a potential conflict. First—despite these initiatives—Japan is still struggling to ramp up defense production. According to the Defense Ministry’s assessments, insufficient parts production is likely to continue limiting the operational availability of military equipment, particularly aircraft, for the Japanese Self-Defense Forces.

This means that Japan is still struggling to meet peacetime demand, let alone the surge in production that a protracted conflict would require. Tokyo is considering government-owned, contractor-operated facilities as a means to enable rapid defense production increases when needed, but the feasibility and potential scale of such agreements remain unclear. This problem is exacerbated by the absence of a legal framework that would allow the government to compel manufacturers to sustain operations in wartime, raising fundamental questions about Tokyo’s ability to translate expanded capacity into wartime output.

Industry observers note that second, Japan’s defense supply chain remains vulnerable. It is extensive and stretched thin, including around 1,100 manufacturers involved in the production of fighter jets, 1,300 for tanks, and 8,300 for destroyers. Despite Tokyo’s efforts to enhance its defense capability, protecting this extensive network remains challenging. In many cases, it is difficult to find alternative suppliers for specialized component materials or specific manufacturing processes. Consequently, disruption to any part of the supply chain could affect the stable supply and maintenance of equipment.

According to recent reports, strengthening supply-chain resilience, particularly with regard to small and medium suppliers, is crucial to ensuring a stable supply of equipment. Tokyo is considering dispersing, hardening, and placing military facilities underground, but these discussions do not apply to industrial suppliers. Increasing supply-chain redundancy—both domestically and with Japan’s strategic partners—is also critical.

According to recent reports, in this respect, the deal with Australia for upgraded Mogami-class frigates, as well as discussions with Indonesia on transferring used Asagiri-class destroyers there, include cooperation on maintenance. Foreign-based maintenance facilities for Japanese-built platforms could, over time, provide additional repair capacity outside Japan.

Sources indicate that the revision of Japan’s three national strategic documents and the Defense Industry Policy is expected to be concluded next month. The policies set out in these documents will determine the course of Japan’s defense industrial policy in the years to come. If production capacity in a protracted conflict is now part of Tokyo’s deterrence calculations, then the test for the strategy documents to be released in December will be whether they move beyond only peacetime capacity. This would entail granting the government the authority to direct production during wartime and planning how civilian manufacturers, particularly in dual-use sectors, could contribute to a wartime surge. Alongside these policies, effective strategic communication to shape an adversary’s expectations about the duration and likely outcome of a conflict will be key to strengthening deterrence.

Jumpei Ishimaru is a research analyst in the Japan program at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

In a recent development, the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Massive Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

Industry observers note that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

In a recent development, on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for prepares purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust newly introduced majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

When U.S. President Donald Trump touches down in Shenzhen, China, this week for a three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, he will be embarking on the highest-level diplomacy he has ever undertaken at his weakest point in power.

The problem is not merely the devastating midterm election losses for his Republican Party, in which he urged supporters to turn out and cast their votes as if he were on the ballot. In recent weeks, Trump has displayed startling latest levels of incoherence and evasion of responsibility for a sitting president. This seemed to reach a crescendo last week with two national crises for which Trump had no suitable answers.

Sources indicate that when U.S. President Donald Trump touches down in Shenzhen, China, this week for a three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, he will be embarking on the highest-level diplomacy he has ever undertaken at his weakest point in power.

In a recent development, the problem is not merely the devastating midterm election losses for his Republican Party, in which he urged supporters to turn out and cast their votes as if he were on the ballot. In recent weeks, Trump has displayed startling fresh levels of incoherence and evasion of responsibility for a sitting president. This seemed to reach a crescendo last week with two national crises for which Trump had no suitable answers.

It has been revealed that the first of these crises brought news that Jensen Huang, the head of Nvidia, at once one of the world’s most valuable and strategically vital companies, had had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Trump pleaded ignorance, denying well-sourced reports that he had been briefed about the matter as long ago as May, including by his national security advisor and secretary of state, Marco Rubio. The only thoughts the president seemed able to summon reflected credulity about Huang’s claim that he had never suspected the woman could have been a spy and personal sympathy for a man who had, until his sudden resignation from Nvidia last week, belonged to a club that means more to Trump than any other: the exclusive circle of the world’s richest and most powerful men. Perhaps for that reason, on Monday, Trump told reporters he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated.

Sources indicate that for all of Trump’s envy of powerful authoritarians, if the situations were reversed and Huang were a Chinese national leading a company as important as Nvidia, it is impossible to imagine Xi treating a man under such suspicions this way, including welcoming him on a flight to his country’s No. 1 competitor and adversary. But Trump’s need for this kind of validation is an ongoing matter and not something he has learned a lesson from. Witness his decision to invite the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to join him on this trip, if not in the meetings with his fellow heads of state.

It has been revealed that for a U.S. president heading off to a summit such as this, the week’s second crisis may have been even worse. The image the United States presented to the world in the wake of a breakdown in the nationwide air traffic control system on Friday was one of utter dishevelment and incompetence. It put the spotlight on two of arguably the least qualified members of a cabinet resolutely hostile to meritocracy: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, a former congressman and Fox News personality, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former congressman whose formal education culminated with an associate’s degree in plumbing and construction.

According to recent reports, with thousands of flights canceled and a country desperate for answers and reassurance, they bumbled their way through an almost incoherent news conference that offered no real explanations. Instead, they cast blame on others, including Congress and past administrations, while exalting Trump’s leadership as if they were members of a personality cult and the public should be too. During the first 36 hours of the crisis, Trump for his part chose to lie low, making no statements about the matter, apparently fearing that doing so would mean taking responsibility for something bad that happened on his watch, which he has always been deeply allergic to.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. president will visit the Philippines and China fresh off his party’s midterm defeat.

Political instability is more danger than opportunity for Beijing.

The Nvidia scandal could upend a fragile consensus in Washington.

These displays of unaccountable behavior and cluelessness are bad enough for the United States in their own right, but Americans should be worried about their implications for the upcoming summit. Even in ordinary times, Trump’s narcissism and emotional neediness make diplomacy like this dangerous because he craves fellowship and approval from men such as Putin and Xi, whom he all but openly idolizes. But with last week’s crises and domestic scandals sprouting in many directions as Democrats prepare to take over Congress, Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency. The cliché holds that weakened or trapped animals are liable to strike out to defend themselves. With Trump, the danger is the opposite—given his self-centered view of the world, where his own ego gratification is paramount, he could give away the store.

Sources indicate that what could that mean? Here, one feels that Trump is so easily flattered that the sky is almost the limit. He has reportedly already forsworn raising the Nvidia crisis with Xi as well as Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine. If true, such self-imposed restrictions themselves emphasize the weakness of the U.S. president’s hand and preemptively vitiate the utility of such an unusual gathering.

Sources indicate that what does this leave on the table for discussion? The Trump administration has said it hopes to make progress on limiting nuclear weapons armament at a time when the United States and Russia still have enormous legacy arsenals whose maintenance and modernization are costly and China is belatedly racing to catch up. Trump officials have also said they hope to engage leaders of the world’s other two big powers on the United States’ stop-and-go war against Iran, which by now has turned into a quagmire.

In a recent development, but what could the latter possibly yield? That Trump has already displayed weakness and enormous gullibility on Iran in his dealings with both powers does not bode well. Russia has supplied intelligence and munitions support to Iran throughout the war, enabling that country to target U.S. military bases throughout the Middle East with devastating effect. Consistent with his general enthrallment to Putin, Trump has publicly downplayed the importance of this, making clear that maintaining warm relations with Moscow is his priority. China, if more cautious than Russia, has also hewed to a line that has enhanced the Iranian state’s position. It has done this by continuing to purchase as much Iranian oil as it can while also reportedly supplying electronic components essential to that country’s missile and drone production. Genuine progress toward administration goals on Iran would require concrete commitments from both powers to stop what they are currently doing. Trump appears unlikely to demand this, and even if he did, neither is likely to follow through.

Industry observers note that putin has already mesmerized Trump into treating Ukraine as if it were the faulty party in its defensive war against Russia. That conflict may not officially be on the agenda when the three leaders sit down together on Thursday, but the specific danger in Shenzhen is that Putin will offer Trump a vague, unverifiable promise to limit support for Iran—something that Trump can present as a win—in exchange for Trump’s deeper complicity in ending the Ukraine war on Russian terms. It would be a trade of something real and irreversible for something hollow and unenforceable. Because of Trump’s unique weakness for glad-handing and grandiosity, it may take little more than that. A more lucid and competent U.S. president would never allow such confusion between the two crises.

What might Xi seek, and how do Trump’s growing vulnerabilities play into this? Beijing’s biggest goal is progress toward exerting control over Taiwan, if not taking over the island altogether by the eventual end of Xi’s longtime hold on power. Toward this end, Trump has already gifted Xi in notable ways without receiving anything in return. At the level of official rhetoric, Trump has weakened America’s traditional support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute between Beijing and Taipei over the island’s future. In fact, he has come close to saying the United States would have no business defending Taiwan in case a war broke out between the two sides.

This by itself is an immense gift, and it would be enhanced further if Trump delayed arms sales to Taiwan to ingratiate himself with Xi. Already, the U.S. military posture in East Asia has been dramatically weakened by the prolonged deployment of aircraft carrier battle groups near Iran and by heavy depletion of advanced weapons systems during the war with that country. Trump has also weakened U.S. alliances in Asia through tariff demands and unpredictable behavior. By nature, Xi seems much more cautious than Putin. But sensing Trump’s weakness and need for some kind of foreign-policy achievement, however illusory, he could try to induce concessions through displays of strongman camaraderie and vague pledges of cooperation in areas of U.S. need.

If we cannot know in advance what these meetings will produce, we should know one thing already. Trump will emerge from them making great claims about how well he gets along with the world’s two other most powerful heads of state. In fact, nothing more might publicly come out of the meetings beyond this. But the world should be wary even of any quiet understandings that Trump, at this moment of extreme weakness and vulnerability, believes he has reached. The likelihood is that he is being played due to his personal and political need, and if the details are unknowable, the costs could be great.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

Recent findings suggest that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Recent findings suggest that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an crucial part of it.”.

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” mentioned Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley stated that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

It has been revealed that “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley noted. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very tech giant that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

A spokesperson for Roblox noted in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place people under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

Recent findings suggest that myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

Recent findings suggest that the modern Middle East was heavily shaped by outside great powers. The victorious World War I allies carved fresh states out of the collapsing Ottoman Empire at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, after making a lot of contradictory promises to various contenders during the war itself. Britain and France governed what is now Lebanon, Iraq, Israel, Syria, and Jordan for most of the interwar period, under mandates from the League of Nations, but the local inhabitants were increasingly restive even before World War II broke out and made it impossible for European powers to retain control. Saudi Arabia gained independence on its own, while Britain provided security for the smaller states in the Gulf. Active support from various outside powers—and especially the United States—was instrumental in Israel’s creation in 1948. Britain and the United States connived to topple the democratic government of Iran in 1953. And the Soviet decision to send arms to Egypt and Syria in the mid-1950s helped cause the 1956 Suez crisis and made the Middle East a central arena in the Cold War.

For the next 35 years, the United States and Soviet Union armed their respective clients, toppled (or tried to topple) regimes they perceived as hostile, and sometimes intervened directly, albeit in mostly limited ways and only for short periods. The United States and USSR also worked together to impose cease-fires to end the recurring wars between Israel and its neighbors, but joint efforts to fashion a broader regional peace were consistently sacrificed on the altar of great-power rivalry.

The end of the Cold War didn’t end great-power meddling, but now it was the United States acting on its own. The first Bush administration organized the coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait in 1991, sponsored the Madrid Conference of 1991, took charge of (and mismanaged) the Oslo peace process, adopted a strategy of dual containment that helped pave the road to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, and then tried to transform the entire region by toppling Saddam Hussein in 2003. We all know how that misguided adventure turned out. U.S. President Donald Trump’s current war with Iran can be seen the last gasp of this hubristic endeavor, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acting as cheerleader, a role he first assumed in 2002. (Regrettably, his forecasts back then were no better than his predictions in 2026).

Like a flash of lightning, the war with Iran has illuminated the new strategic landscape. The failed U.S. interventions in Iraq and Libya (along with Russia’s inability to prevent the eventual toppling of Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad) reveals new limits to what outside military power can accomplish. Similarly, Iran’s ability to resist decades of U.S. pressure and acquire a large arsenal of missiles and drones, plus mastery of the nuclear fuel cycle, further underscore the declining efficacy of outside intervention. Saudi Arabia’s lavishly funded military couldn’t bomb its way to victory over the Houthis in Yemen, and Israel’s repeated and increasingly ferocious assaults against its various opponents did not prevent Hamas from mounting a major attack in October 2023 or fully eliminate either Hamas or Hezbollah. Even before the war with Iran, in short, the limits of military power (and especially when wielded by states outside the region) were becoming clear.

Today, the combination of cheap but lethal drones and more sophisticated ballistic missiles has raised the cost of external military intervention to new heights. Not only did weeks of punishing air strikes fail to topple Iran’s regime, but the United States proved unable to protect its own bases in the region from Iranian retaliation. The damage to these facilities has made sustained military action in the region more difficult and expensive; for example, U.S. aircraft carriers cannot safely operate close to Iran, which reduces loiter times for attack aircraft and the payloads they can carry. Nor can the United States protect its local clients from being attacked, except by using lots of expensive interceptors (e.g. Patriot missiles) that are far more expensive than the missiles and drones they are shooting down and are in increasingly short supply. Nor are Patriots or systems like Israel’s Iron Dome impenetrable, especially when an adversary can fire lots of drones or missiles at once.

The limits of airpower have been apparent for a long time (although that reality is often ignored by political leaders eager to “do something”), but these new technologies are also making ground invasions increasingly unattractive. As we have seen in Ukraine, assembling large ground units exposes them to deadly drone or missile strikes, which is why loose talk about the United States invading Iran is not to be taken seriously. Iran may be deeply divided, and its government may be unpopular, but the occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan should have taught Americans by now that trying to invade and control a country of 80 million people is a very bad idea.

The bottom line is that the days when mighty great powers could intervene in the Middle East with near-impunity—as the United States did during Desert Storm in 1991—are behind us.

According to recent reports, A second trend—the declining importance of Middle East energy—will reinforce the first. That might seem like an odd statement at present, given the sharp rise in fuel prices caused by the war, but most of these price rises are due to limited refining capacity (a problem exacerbated by the Iran war and the war in Ukraine) and not the supply of crude oil itself. The relative importance of Middle East energy has been declining significantly since 1973, when a Saudi-led boycott sent prices soaring and led to long gas lines in the United States. Since then, the shale oil boom in the United States and broader global efforts to address climate change by reducing fossil fuel consumption have made Middle East oil less critical than it used to be. That is why Middle Eastern countries like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are trying to diversify their own economies. They know that the days of oil and gas exports being able to pay all the bills are rapidly waning.

Industry observers note that note: I am not saying that energy (and fertilizer) supplies from the Middle East will be irrelevant, only that they will be much less critical in the future than they have been in the past. In short, the need to intervene in the region to safeguard energy exports is declining while the cost of trying to do so is rising. Put these two trends together, and direct military involvement by outside powers is much less attractive.

According to recent reports, for the first time in more than a century, therefore, one can envision a Middle East whose fate is determined primarily by the peoples in the region and not by outsiders. Distant great powers will still have dealings with different Middle East states (such as selling arms, pursuing investments and trade arrangements, etc.) but local governments will have the initiative. What should we expect them to do?

In a recent development, for starters, I’d expect a lot of good, old-fashioned balance-of-power politics, where ideologies and sectarian differences matter little and the need to keep the strongest powers in check will drive an ever-shifting array of regional coalitions. At the same time, such a pattern does not preclude renewed efforts to lower tensions between Iran, Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, and others, and perhaps even to negotiate a broader security architecture for the region that doesn’t depend on great-power support. The United States will revert to its former role as an “offshore balancer,” reduce its military footprint there, and pursue more businesslike relations with everyone in the region instead of “special relationships” with a few. In other words, it will act more like China. And if outside powers are no longer willing or able to provide protection, then more Middle Eastern states will be tempted to acquire a nuclear deterrent and the risk of preventive wars to thwart such efforts is likely to grow, as well.

One can also speculate on how these developments will affect the internal politics of some of these states. If Middle Eastern countries must rely primarily on their own resources and strategies for security and defense, they will have to get better at mobilizing real military power instead of just buying a lot of expensive toys from foreign defense contractors. But as King Farouk of Egypt or King Feisal II of Iraq could have told you, creating more potent military forces is risky in top-down societies ruled by privileged elites, because the guardians of their power may want more of a say in how things are run. For this reason, the emergence of a more autonomous Middle East could also usher in a newly introduced era of internal political turmoil.

The bottom line: We may be approaching the end of foreign efforts to remake the Middle East, but don’t expect the region to become boring.

Sources indicate that stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The Upcoming Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world.
