Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
  • The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five fresh air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

Sources indicate that they justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it swiftly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization blueprint so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

According to recent reports, senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz remarked that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

According to recent reports, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

Sources indicate that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott remarked, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not significant on government running things.”.

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he stated. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

In a recent development, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

Sources indicate that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy stated. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create concerns in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

In a recent development, the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

According to recent reports, the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that bedford noted he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, European priorities for Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen.

In a recent development, on the heels of a disappointing U.S. midterm election for the Republican Party, President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday for a week of high-stakes meetings with the Indo-Pacific’s biggest powers. From security talks with old allies to historic summits with foreign adversaries, Trump will be reengaging with a region that has largely been relegated to the back burner during his second term.

Recent findings suggest that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, European priorities for Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen.

On the heels of a disappointing U.S. midterm election for the Republican Party, President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday for a week of high-stakes meetings with the Indo-Pacific’s biggest powers. From security talks with old allies to historic summits with foreign adversaries, Trump will be reengaging with a region that has largely been relegated to the back burner during his second term.

According to recent reports, trump’s trip kicks off in Manila, Philippines, where he will join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Tuesday to discuss some of the greatest threats to the region, including how wars in Iran and Ukraine have impacted the bloc’s economic security. During that time, Trump will also hold in-person talks with his fellow Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders—Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi—for the first time since taking office nearly two years ago.

Meeting with the Quad will offer several opportunities for pomp and pageantry; however, experts expect little substance to come out of the summit. “I don’t think the president can hide the fact that he’s not terribly enthusiastic about the gathering,” Kurt Campbell, the co-founder of the Asia Group, a Washington-based geopolitical advisory firm, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar. Instead, the talks will likely serve as a box-checking exercise before Trump can turn his attention to other matters—namely, China.

In a recent development, after less than 24 hours in the Philippines, Trump will head to the Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. While there, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet one-on-one with an eye toward maintaining the status quo. That will likely include talks on critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and their recently extended trade truce. Last week’s Nvidia scandal, though, is almost certainly off the table.

The summit’s timing is consequential, as the U.S. midterms reckoning may have shifted Xi’s perception of the Trump administration as it enters its lame-duck period. “Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments,” Deng Yuwen argued in Foreign Policy.

Trump, however, may be hoping to challenge that perception with several sideline summits.

On Thursday, he will meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin for what China’s Foreign Ministry has called a meeting of “groundbreaking significance.” Although senior administration officials told reporters on Friday that Trump would not bring up the Russia-Ukraine war at the trilateral dialogue, those talks are now expected to discuss the conflict as well as push for denuclearization, though Xi will likely try to rebuff efforts to debate nuclear arms.

In a recent development, trump has also suggested that he might hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin, reversing previous assurances from his staff that he had no aims to do so. And he has floated a potential meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Shenzhen trip—again, defying past administration claims that talks with Kim were not in the cards.

“We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come. I don’t know—that’s up to President Xi,” Trump told reporters on Monday. Such talks would also likely center on Pyongyang’s nuclear program.

Tuesday, Nov. 17: Xi separately hosts Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori.

Takaichi holds bilateral talks with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

European Union defense ministers convene in Brussels.

Israel’s Knesset is set to debate and vote on a new speaker.

Thursday, Nov. 19: The International Court of Justice rules in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslims.

Friday, Nov. 20: Takaichi hosts Fujimori.

Brussels hosts the second EU-U.K. leaders’ summit.

Industry observers note that monday, Nov. 23: Polish President Karol Nawrocki begins a five-day trip to Argentina and Chile.

Priority No. 1. The European Union accused Russia on Monday of trying to drag out peace talks while continuing to target Ukraine’s power grid ahead of what is expected to be another harsh winter. “We actually don’t have a cease-fire, and they continue to weaken Ukraine and kill people every single day,” EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas mentioned.

Sources indicate that EU leaders also warned against discussing the future of European security with Russia before an immediate truce is reached, stressed that Moscow should be the one to make concessions since Russia began the war, and insisted that EU leaders are prepared to reject any fresh demands from the Kremlin. “We don’t need a newly introduced security architecture. We need to restore the one we have,” Kallas stated. “Russia has broken all the treaties that underpin it.”.

According to recent reports, to reiterate that point, the EU imposed fresh sanctions on Monday targeting nearly 50 Russian financial institutions as well as business executives involved in the energy and oil industries, including Tatyana Kim, the founder of retail giant Wildberries. The bloc also issued fresh asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of people accused of spreading disinformation and pro-Russian propaganda.

Recent findings suggest that the EU’s actions come just days after Putin agreed to allow European representatives to join future Russia-Ukraine peace talks. The EU decided on Friday that its delegation will comprise five major military powers—nonmember Britain as well as France, ‌Germany, Italy, and Poland—and EU institutions.

Military retreat. Saudi Arabia on Monday replaced the commander overseeing its anti-Houthi operations after its Yemeni allies were forced to withdraw from large swaths of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. The retreat marked a significant blow to the Saudi-backed coalition, as the fighters characterized the move—which they described as a redeployment—as necessary to protect the interim capital of Aden.

It has been revealed that for months, the Iran-backed Houthis have advanced on the Red Sea and targeted critical energy infrastructure. In October, Yemen’s internationally recognized, Saudi-supported government launched “Dawn of Yemen,” a major counteroffensive aimed at retaking that territory.

But the coalition’s successes have been limited. According to Yemen’s military on Monday, the Houthis ​have now advanced to the southern coastal area of Khor Omairh and are ⁠just 16 miles from government lines at the fishing village of Qawah. That has forced Saudi-backed Yemeni fighters to focus their attention on defending their base of operations in Aden as well as breaking the Houthis’ siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

In a recent development, same-day killings. Separate mass shootings in South Africa over the weekend killed at least 17 people, local police confirmed on Monday. Although the country has struggled to rein in violent crime for years, there has been a recent surge in mass shootings with high fatality rates across the country.

On Sunday, South African authorities found eight bodies in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle outside the city of Pietermaritzburg; efforts to identify the individuals and establish a possible motive remain ongoing. Hours later, police discovered nine people killed by gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville, located near the country’s capital. Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni remarked that the Jeffsville killings could be related to a shooting at a nearby settlement last year that killed 12 people and injured 13 others, as one of the people killed on Sunday was a “person of interest” in the previous shooting.

The same-day incidents, occurring 330 miles apart, bring the total number of major mass shootings in South Africa to nine since December 2025. Of those, the deadliest was a shooting at a bar in Johannesburg in September that killed 18 people; that killing was one of three mass casualty shootings in the span of a week. South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates in the world.

Fun for the British royal family isn’t just polo matches and chauffeur-driven motorcades. On Monday, Prince William and Princess Catherine kicked off their three-day trip to India with a game of gully cricket in the city of Mumbai. After fielding balls with local children and retired cricketer Sachin Tendulkar, the couple took a ride on the city’s metro rail system to promote the two countries’ close economic ties. This was their first joint visit to India in roughly a decade, and it was the princess’s most high-profile overseas trip since undergoing cancer treatment in 2024.

Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
  • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
  • The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

Recent findings suggest that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

Several senators leaving the meeting noted the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., mentioned Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, mentioned, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she mentioned.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday stated at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

It has been revealed that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Industry observers note that A colleague in the intelligence community once jokingly called me a “Chinese spy.” His casual remark is burned into my memory. I am a Taiwanese American who has served as a U.S. intelligence officer and worked on semiconductor policy for the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Even while serving this country, my loyalty could become a punchline.

Recent findings suggest that the Jensen Huang scandal now tests Washington’s ability to keep that reflex out of national security policy. He resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Nov. 12, just days after reports of his relationships with businesswoman Alice Huang and a firm executive. Yet his abrupt departure leaves serious questions related to Chinese espionage unresolved. Investigators must still determine whether Jensen Huang helped Beijing obtain secrets or influence.

According to recent reports, in the meantime, public discourse in the United States is conflating the potential for Chinese coercion with the proof of its existence, even going so far as to promote ethnic scapegoating. The growing hysteria is increasingly focused on the threat posed by anyone at all associated with China. The irony is that this will eventually, in concrete ways, make Americans less secure.

News reports described intercepted communications suggesting that Chinese intelligence received information from someone close to Jensen Huang and Nvidia. It also reported that federal officials have been investigating whether Alice Huang’s Megaspeed has been potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China since 2024. If true, Washington should prosecute those involved and close relevant loopholes.

Recent findings suggest that reporting has also described, however, a troubling divide within the U.S. government. Some intelligence officials considered the spy label “over-torqued.” Attorney General Todd Blanche and Rep. Jim Himes, a ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, also weighed in on the day that Jensen Huang resigned, saying neither the U.S. Justice Department nor the intelligence community had concluded she was a spy; while her reported proximity to Jensen Huang justifies scrutiny, it cannot by itself prove that she worked for Beijing.

In a recent development, either way, nothing about this case makes all people of Asian descent suspect. Jensen Huang’s conduct deserves scrutiny; the loyalty of millions who share his ancestry does not. And yet Congress is beginning to overstep from proper oversight into broader exclusion. Rep. Riley Moore’s bill, for example, proposes denying student and exchange visas for research or study to Chinese nationals. Adopting that approach in response to Nvidia solely because of someone’s nationality fails to address actual security vulnerabilities.

Washington could and should proactively mitigate threats; foreign intelligence ties, risky financial exposure, and transferring unauthorized information are legitimate reasons to restrict sensitive access. But the idea that every Chinese citizen could be a spy dangerously conflates vulnerability with culpability.

Recent findings suggest that it’s true that China’s national intelligence law compels citizens and organizations to assist intelligence work. Beijing can pressure its citizens, but that does not automatically make them a Chinese agent. In 2018, William Evanina, then the United States’ top counterintelligence official, noted that 99.9 percent of Chinese students in the United States were “here legitimately and doing great research.” Most may never be approached by China’s Ministry of State Security, and others might simply refuse or report such encounters. Effective counterintelligence cannot consider these all as equivalent.

The current public discourse is also actively blurring the clear distinction between Chinese ancestry and Chinese citizenship. The Asian American Journalists Association called out headlines that turned Jensen Huang’s surname into an espionage pun. On X, a viral collage highlighted prominent executives married to women of Chinese descent with the caption, “I have one question… actually, a LOT of questions.” Another post invoked “Chinese honeypot espionage” in reference to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s former roommate, Chinese American AI executive Alexandr Wang.

In a recent development, in a 2019 bill that Trump signed into law, Congress warned that profiling plays right into Beijing’s narrative that the global Chinese diaspora owes it loyalty. Washington should not validate that claim.

Blanket suspicion makes legitimate threats harder to identify. MITRE’s insider threat researchers warned that indiscriminate threat indicators overwhelm security with false positives. Nationality alone cannot distinguish a Chinese agent from a dissident resisting Beijing. Pursuing imagined spies can leave real ones undetected.

Recent findings suggest that profiling also silences those best positioned to expose espionage. The FBI warns of various ways that foreign governments may coerce their citizens in the United States to serve their interests. A threatened scientist could help investigators neutralize foreign intelligence activity early. If speaking up invites suspicion, though, they will likely remain silent.

Trust is critical to improving security. In April 2025, Taiwan’s Defense Ministry found that voluntary reporting prompted 87.5 percent of national security investigations. Beijing’s preferred targets are often best positioned to expose its operations. Washington should make reporting foreign coercion safer through confidential channels backed by legal and security assistance.

It has been revealed that unwarranted suspicion also threatens the United States’ AI talent lead over China. A recent study by Carnegie Endowment found that 57 percent of authors accepted to NeurIPS 2025, one of the most elite AI conferences, had earned undergraduate degrees in China. Only 13 percent had gone to college in the United States. Furthermore, China now hosts 41 percent of the world’s top AI researchers. The United States is down to 34 percent, flipping its 2022 advantage. Washington cannot afford to alienate these scientists.

A 2023 study found that 89 percent of Chinese researchers at U.S. universities desired American scientific leadership, yet nearly two-thirds had considered leaving the country. The United States risks losing the scientists who want to help it lead. Treating them as presumptive threats could hand the U.S. talent advantage to Beijing.

The United States has made this mistake before. In 1950, Washington stripped Qian Xuesen, one of the country’s leading rocket scientists, of his security clearance. The FBI suspected that he was tied to communists but failed to uncover evidence of espionage. Due to his rocketry expertise, however, security officials struggled between deporting or detaining him. When Qian finally left in 1955, he spearheaded China’s formidable missile and space programs. Washington considered him too dangerous to trust and too valuable to let go. It lost him anyway.

It has been revealed that before pursuing charges or major research sanctions, security officers should mandate independent technical review and offer researchers due process, presuming innocence until proven guilty. In 2015, prosecutors charged Temple University physicist Xiaoxing Xi with sending proprietary technology to China. They eventually dropped the case after finding that he actually shared nonsensitive devices, but his reputation was already destroyed.

In a recent development, congress already requires that federal research agencies avoid discriminating based on race, ethnicity, or national origin. Yet a January 2026 Government Accountability Office report found that five major agencies had still not evaluated their anti-discrimination safeguards. Washington should conduct those assessments to ensure all researchers are equally scrutinized based on their conduct.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang’s successes and failures do not make Asian Americans more or less American. Washington can and should investigate espionage without ethnically profiling Asian Americans. Otherwise, the United States risks overlooking real spies, silencing whistleblowers, and driving away world-class talent. The country’s great strength is its ability to distinguish friend from foe. It cannot afford to confuse the two.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Industry observers note that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

Sources indicate that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

In a recent development, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

It has been revealed that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

Recent findings suggest that in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

According to recent reports, the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Industry observers note that power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

Industry observers note that the United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

Power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

It has been revealed that the United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

That’s about double the generation capacity of the entire U.S. grid. If even a fraction of this can be added, it would push down energy prices for companies and consumers alike.

This backlog, which is largely a function of limited high-capacity transmission lines and delays in federal permitting, isn’t simply an economic problem—it’s a national security risk for the United States, which is falling dangerously behind China in its rate of electrification. According to Grid Strategies, between 2021 and 2025 China built on average about 14,800 miles of high-capacity transmission per year while the United States built only 400 miles a year. The United States cannot expect to compete successfully with China in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, or defense production without expanding its ability to generate, transmit, and reliably deliver electricity.

Critiques of the U.S. permitting process have reached a crescendo in recent years, memorialized in books such as Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s Abundance and Dan Wang’s Breakneck: China’s Quest to Engineer the Future, which contrasts America’s legal culture with China’s engineer-led society. This indictment of the U.S. inability to build has adherents on the left and right, making it the rare policy area where there is the prospect of bipartisan cooperation. There’s even a “Build America” caucus in the House of Representatives focused on enhancing and expanding U.S. infrastructure.

But until recently, it looked as if permitting reform would remain a legislative pipe dream. The Trump administration’s animosity to renewable energy made it unlikely that Democrats would trust President Donald Trump to apply enhanced permitting powers evenhandedly. However, on Sept. 30, Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse alongside Republican Sens. Mike Lee and Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. The since revised 494-page bill, which is slated for amendment and a vote on final passage in the Senate this week, would revolutionize how energy infrastructure gets built and paid for in the United States, including AI data centers.

Industry observers note that the bill aims to accelerate approvals for high-voltage transmission lines and the permitting of individual projects in several ways. First, it would speed up interstate transmission by putting into statute previous guidance from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which requires grid operators to standardize regional and joint interregional transmission planning processes.

Under BAAJA, if state or local grid operators failed to act on developers’ applications within a year, FERC would have the ability to approve vital interstate power lines. Proponents of clean energy see these provisions as critical to increasing the share of renewables in the national energy mix. Solar and wind energy often need to be transmitted from where they are generated—open, rural land, or offshore—to where the demand is: cities and technology and manufacturing hubs.

The bill also sets limits on which projects require review under the National Environmental Policy Act and would speed up the process for both agency review and citizen lawsuits, which Heinrich described as a “shot clock.” This is the part of the bill that worries environmentalists the most, as it would reduce citizens’ ability to employ the courts to delay, and exercise oversight of, energy projects.

Sources indicate that responding to concerns that data centers are driving up consumers’ utility rates, the bill would require data centers to pay the full cost of the energy they are drawing from the existing grid, as well as the expense of expanding grid capacity for their further build-out. Because their primary objective has been the speed with which they can gain assured access to power, data centers have been increasingly installing noisy, polluting, and expensive off-grid natural gas generators to run their operations.

Industry observers note that doing away with these climate-damaging “behind the meter” approaches by requiring data centers to draw power from the grid itself is one area where we’d like to see this bill improved—or fixed by subsequent legislation. But advocates believe the additional energy supply that BAAJA would unlock would increasingly bring data centers into the grid without the need for further legislative intervention.

Finally, the bill’s language on permitting certainty would limit the federal government’s ability to cancel projects from sources of electricity it opposes. If compared with the previous 10 years developers can show a pattern of disparate treatment of their class of projects, whether renewables or fossil fuels, they can sue and recover costs.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, the bill still includes a provision that would empower the current administration, or future governments, to block or rescind permits for specific projects upon asserting that they would be harmful for U.S. national security. This sort of waiver language is common to much of the legislation that Congress passes. Under normal circumstances, this is a reasonable ask, but the current administration has abused these mechanisms to target renewable energy projects, especially wind generation, without explanation.

Sources indicate that at present, the Defense Department runs a Siting Clearinghouse that reviews proposed energy projects to ensure they don’t interfere with military readiness, training, flight paths, radar, or testing. Over the past two years, the Trump administration has stalled its review of hundreds of wind projects, including at least 35 that had already undergone the review process and were just waiting on a final signature from department officials. When courts found these delays to be without justification, the administration offered developers some $4 billion to cancel their projects anyway. Clean energy backers argue that this de facto moratorium on processing reviews for a particular class of projects is without precedent.

If the Trump administration intends to use national security arguments to delay or obstruct renewables projects even if BAAJA passes, as his recent remarks on the topic would suggest, the expectation that renewables will fare better under a newly introduced permitting regime becomes less convincing.

Thankfully, there is a potential fix for this situation hiding in another important piece of legislation that Congress will take up in the lame-duck session: the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Both the House and the Senate versions of the bill include language that would impose a 180-day shot clock for national security reviews to be completed, which would provide the private sector clearer planning and cost timelines. The Senate’s bill would also require the Defense Department to articulate and defend its rationale for denying any project’s permit on national security grounds.

If enacted, this NDAA provision could allay the fears of some Democrats—including former President Joe Biden’s climate czar John Podesta—that the Trump administration will weaponize BAAJA to favor fossil fuels rather than facilitating a fair contest between oil and gas and competing energy solutions.

Ultimately, the U.S. energy system is critical infrastructure. Its scale and reliability affect military installations, communications networks, transportation, financial services, industrial facilities—essentially every important component of modern society. BAAJA isn’t a perfect bill, but it should provide a path for increasing energy availability, reducing costs, and accelerating the clean energy transition, especially if the NDAA enacts safeguards on the abuse of national security exceptions. America’s strategic position may be teetering under the Trump administration, but in this age of electrification, BAAJA would enable the country to start building again—and that will increase U.S. prosperity and security alike.

Industry observers note that josh Busby is a professor of public affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and former senior climate advisor at the U.S. Defense Department. He is the author of States and Nature: The Effects of Climate Change on Security, which was the winner of 2026 Grawemeyer Award for Ideas Advancing World Order.

Greg Pollock is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University, where he teaches graduate students about national security risks. He previously served in a series of leadership positions in the Office of the U.S. Secretary of Defense, most recently as the acting deputy assistant secretary of defense for the Arctic and global resilience policy.

The True Meaning of Power

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “International politics, like all politics, is a struggle for power.” Hans Morgenthau wrote this sentence from his desk in Chicago at the dawn of the Cold War, as the United States and the Soviet Union embarked on an open-ended competition for global dominance.
  • Industry observers note that although much has changed in the nearly eight decades since Morgenthau’s most influential work was published, the fundamentals remain the same.
  • Recent findings suggest that for many, Morgenthau’s contributions begin and end with his identification of power as the key determinant of state behavior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What the Godfather of Realism Can Teach Trump.

Industry observers note that “International politics, like all politics, is a struggle for power.” Hans Morgenthau wrote this sentence from his desk in Chicago at the dawn of the Cold War, as the United States and the Soviet Union embarked on an open-ended competition for global dominance. Politics Among Nations, the volume that Morgenthau ultimately produced, would rapidly become the most widely adopted international relations textbook in the United States and provide an intellectual framework—realism—that would guide generations of scholars and policymakers.

Industry observers note that although much has changed in the nearly eight decades since Morgenthau’s most influential work was published, the fundamentals remain the same. Human nature, which for Morgenthau drove the struggle for power, is unmoved. States are still the most significant actors in the international system and compete for influence. Great powers continue to drive the course of history. Much of today’s world would seem to affirm Morgenthau’s conclusions: Russia’s attempts to establish a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe, China’s quest for hegemony in East Asia, and the United States’ revival of the Monroe Doctrine in the Western Hemisphere all suggest the enduring primacy of national interests over moral aspirations and international norms.

Recent findings suggest that for many, Morgenthau’s contributions begin and end with his identification of power as the key determinant of state behavior. But this reading misses one of his core observations: that even if humans tend to be power-maximizing creatures, they are also moral beings who seek to limit their own power. Morgenthau’s writings reveal a dialectic between power and morality—two seemingly incompatible concepts that he spent his life attempting to reconcile. Far from romanticizing power, Morgenthau saw the need to tame it.

Industry observers note that an immigrant who escaped Nazi Germany and owed his life to the United States, Morgenthau had specific guidance to offer his fellow Americans. Even as he urged the United States to protect its vital interests by maintaining a favorable balance of power in key regions, he implored the country to wield its power prudently. Morgenthau saw the United States as the only country with both the capacity and the will to fight on behalf of transcendent values that he believed power had to serve. He was committed to preserving American power as a check on the violence and bigotry he experienced. Yet he feared that U.S. overreach would hollow out the foundations of that power. This, for Morgenthau, would be a tragedy for humanity.

Perhaps no government has misread Morgenthau more than the second Trump administration. Its officials revel in the exercise of military force around the world, from Iran to Venezuela and the Caribbean, while dismissing concerns of alleged war crimes and threatening long-standing allies. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller typified the Trumpian outlook when, in January, he invoked the “iron laws of the world,” one “governed by strength,” “governed by force,” and “governed by power.”.

Some analysts have also erroneously rooted the Trump administration’s actions in realism. A lengthy essay in The New York Times Magazine, for instance, ran under the headline “The Theory That Gives Trump a Blank Check for Aggression.” This is understandable, as the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed its actions are underpinned by “flexible realism.”.

It has been revealed that but any reading of realism that does not consider the moral dimensions of Morgenthau’s theory is both mistaken and dangerous. When the United States limits its own power, abiding by international norms, consulting allies and partners, and wielding its strength in pursuit of transcendent values, countries find American influence more palatable, which helps sustain it. But if Washington’s actions become untethered from these restraints, others will no longer defer to American prerogatives, and the world will become a more dangerous place.

Recent findings suggest that returning to the foundations of realism—to the man who introduced this intellectual tradition to Americans—is critical. If Morgenthau were to witness this moment in U.S. history, he would conclude that the country had overlearned his lessons about the importance of power and erred in equating it with the use of force. He would see a need to elevate moral questions and rebuild normative constraints on the exercise of power. And he would warn against foreign entanglements that undermine American democracy, which remains the wellspring of the country’s power. These are the lessons that will help the United States navigate an era of intensified great-power competition, one in which the margin for error is thin and the cost of miscalculation could be catastrophic.

Morgenthau was born into an assimilated, middle-class Jewish family in southern Germany in the winter of 1904. His conservative and authoritarian father, Ludwig, raised his only child to revere the monarchy and take pride in their country’s achievements. Morgenthau’s childhood might have passed as that of a shy, precocious boy in a self-assured bourgeois community, but Germany’s defeat in World War I and the rise of anti-Semitism set his life on a drastically different course.

Industry observers note that in 1922, as a top student in his high school, Morgenthau was chosen to address his classmates and neighbors in a public ceremony honoring the school’s namesake. When he began to speak, he noticed that some had turned their backs and others were holding their noses at this “stinking Jew.” Morgenthau finished his remarks, but as he left the square, his classmates hurled anti-Semitic insults and spat on him. Just months later, Hitler descended on Morgenthau’s hometown of Coburg with hundreds of storm troopers, who assaulted protesters while the police looked on. Coburg soon gained the ignominious distinction of being the first town to elect the Nazis to power.

Sources indicate that morgenthau left Coburg hoping to become a writer or poet but was forced to pivot to law after hyperinflation ruined his family’s finances. During his apprenticeship under Hugo Sinzheimer, a leading left-wing labor lawyer, he saw conservative judges undermine the Weimar Republic and aid those who sought its destruction. Morgenthau later reflected in his intellectual autobiography that this led him to conclude that “what was decisive was not the merits of different legal interpretations but the distribution of political power.”.

In a recent development, as life for German Jews deteriorated, he fled to Geneva to teach law. Switzerland was unfortunately not far enough away; after Hitler took power in Germany, students began boycotting his classes because they did not want to learn German law from a Jew. He then found a teaching position in Madrid but was displaced by the Spanish Civil War and wandered through Europe before arriving in Latest York in 1937 as a penniless refugee. Having witnessed the rise of fascism up close, Morgenthau was shocked to find that so many Americans believed that human nature was fundamentally good, that peace was the normal condition of humanity, and that history was a story of progress.

In a recent development, in Latest York and then Kansas City, Morgenthau grew alarmed as the United States watched Nazi Germany rearm, annex Austria, and invade Czechoslovakia. He believed that a failure to understand human nature had inspired Western democracies’ blind faith in international law and the League of Nations, leading them down the path of least resistance with appeasement of Hitler, straight into the moral abyss.

Sources indicate that shaken by the fall of France in 1940, Morgenthau began writing his first English-language book, taking aim at Americans’ confidence that the methods of the natural sciences could make sense of the social world and that the sheer force of reason would eventually eliminate conflict. In Scientific Man vs. Power Politics, published in 1946, he charged that rationalism and liberalism had misunderstood the nature of man, the nature of the world, and the nature of reason itself. Humans, in addition to having rational needs, possessed irrational impulses that could not be reasoned away. Man’s “lust for power would be satisfied only … if he became like God.” Countries, like humans, sought to maximize their power over one another, making conflict inevitable.

In a recent development, scientific Man received disastrous reviews, and Morgenthau later recalled that it “shocked people to no end.” He adjusted his approach, tailoring his message to Americans and packaging it in a textbook that would appeal to their pragmatism. He wanted this book to mark an evolution in American thinking about foreign policy, privately writing that it would differ from its predecessors “as an automobile differs from a horse and buggy.” Two years later, in Politics Among Nations, he achieved that goal. Morgenthau stressed that the struggle for power was inescapable. All states sought to keep, increase, or demonstrate their strength. Disarmament, collective security, and international law would not contain this struggle. Only a balance of power could prevent countries from attempting to overthrow the existing order. Power could be tamed only by countervailing power.

In a recent development, it is easy to see why many misread Morgenthau as a champion of realpolitik—an heir to the likes of Machiavelli or Bismarck. After all, he placed power at the center of his analysis. But he never romanticized it. As he wrote in a private letter, “I am an analyst of the nation state and of power and have emphasized time and again their negative moral connotations.” Morgenthau’s personal encounters with power had taught him that its unbridled pursuit led to calamity. He understood that normative and moral limitations were required to keep the struggle for power within tolerable bounds. As he wrote in another letter, “It is the task of civilized societies to temper the power drives and direct them into socially useful channels.”.

Industry observers note that indeed, Morgenthau had less tolerance for those who failed to reconcile power with morality than for those who underestimated power’s importance. Although President Woodrow Wilson’s universalism and idealism made him one of Morgenthau’s favorite targets, he preferred him to a Machiavellian prince: “Wilson’s failure was at least the failure of greatness, of too great a vision. Nobody will say as much for the epigones of Machiavelli.” He similarly criticized the British historian and political theorist E. H. Carr, whose moral relativism had led him to advocate for appeasing Hitler. Carr, he wrote, had “no transcendent point of view from which to survey the political scene and to appraise the phenomenon of power.” While both men are seen as pivotal realist thinkers, Morgenthau witheringly concluded of Carr that “it is a dangerous thing to be a Machiavelli. It is a disastrous thing to be a Machiavelli without virtù”—that is, it is ruinous to practice power politics without skill and judgment.

In a recent development, in Politics Among Nations, Morgenthau took concern with leaders who both glorify the struggle for power and reject any limits on their own use of power. He argued that “philosophies and political systems which have made the lust and the struggle for power their mainstay have proved impotent and self-destructive.” And he drew attention to common moral standards that could sustain order and moderate the struggle for power. He observed that throughout history, humans insisted on subjecting political action to ethical scrutiny. When such restraints held, countries did less than their power enabled them to do; once commonplace practices, such as assassinating a rival country’s leaders or killing a large portion of its civilian population to reduce its strength, became stigmatized. Morgenthau concluded, “What has changed is the influence of civilization which makes what is desirable and feasible ethically reprehensible and, hence, normally impossible of execution.”.

Industry observers note that in the immediate aftermath of World War II, however, he believed that the limitations on the struggle for power had reached their weakest point since the advent of the modern state system. Hitler had attempted to extinguish a whole people, and both the Axis and the Allied powers had bombed cities indiscriminately. Although Morgenthau believed the Allies were morally justified in taking such actions to defeat a genocidal regime, he nonetheless feared that the struggle for power was on its way to becoming boundless. In the nuclear age, failing to reestablish these moral barriers could mean the end of humanity.

Recent findings suggest that morgenthau’s hard-nosed reputation has long obscured the moral core of his realism. He was unequivocal that power must be a means to an end—“an attempt to realize moral values through the medium of politics.” He recognized that maximizing power for its own sake was both destructive and pointless, arguing that “a nation must pursue its interests for the sake of a transcendent purpose which gives meaning to the day-to-day operations of its foreign policy.” In his view, ancient Greece and Rome are remembered because their power served a purpose that outlived their empires: Athenian democracy and philosophy, and Roman law and republican government.

As he assimilated and raised a family in Chicago, Morgenthau came to see the United States as the inheritor of this tradition. The country’s contribution to the world and the source of its power lay in its democracy and civic life. A realist approach—one that prudently wielded power abroad—was best suited to protect the American experiment at home, enabling Americans to live in freedom and security while offering an example for other countries to emulate. In other words, American power had to be bound to purpose—a purpose the country fulfilled “as a light to attract strangers, not as a flame to be spread throughout the world.” This was not merely the observation of a dispassionate scholar. The United States had accepted Morgenthau when no other country would, and it was a place where immigrants like him could rise to the top of their fields.

By the 1960s, Morgenthau saw that American power faced a threat of its own making. He began to develop deep misgivings about U.S. intervention in Vietnam, warning as early as 1961 that it could become a quagmire reminiscent of France’s war in Algeria. Two years later, as clashes between the South Vietnamese government and protesters intensified, Morgenthau urged the United States to get out. He built his opposition on realist grounds, arguing that a communist takeover of Vietnam would not affect the balance of power in Asia, thus rejecting the domino theory, which held that communism would spread inexorably outward once it gained a regional foothold. Morgenthau also recognized that communism was no longer monolithic and believed that Ho Chi Minh could lead a nonaligned country as Tito did in Yugoslavia. He saw the conflict as a civil war and worried that the United States was attempting to maintain a status quo that was itself the source of instability.

Successive administrations failed to heed Morgenthau’s warnings and instead plunged the United States deeper into the war. He came to resent American policymakers’ misappropriation of his lessons on power and entered public debate with upcoming vigor. At a packed rally in New York’s Madison Square Garden in June 1965, he warned that a guerrilla war could be won only through the indiscriminate killing of the South Vietnamese people, which would tear at the moral fiber of the United States. Later that month, Morgenthau debated President Lyndon Johnson’s national security adviser, McGeorge Bundy, on national television. He led with his moral outrage: “I am opposed to our present policy in Vietnam on moral, military, political, and general intellectual grounds.”.

The greatest risk of the war, Morgenthau discerned, was “the risk to ourselves, to our mission in the world, to our very existence as a distinct nation.” He lamented, “Here is the last best hope of the downtrodden and the enslaved, to which men of good will throughout the world have looked as a shining example, relieving its frustration in blind ideological fury and aimless destructiveness upon a helpless people.” Vietnam, in his telling, had corrupted the very purpose that gave American power its meaning.

The Vietnam War validated Morgenthau’s belief that power untethered from questions of morality would lead to overreach. It proved that the United States had an interest in constraining itself, if only to avoid disaster. More fundamentally, Vietnam showed that misadventures abroad could boomerang, weakening American democracy and societal cohesion and, ultimately, undermining the country’s international standing.

The second Trump administration’s foreign policy record has thrown these insights into sharp relief. Its officials view questions of morality as a costly sideshow, the remit of woolly-minded idealists who do not understand how the world works. The White House has time and again resorted to military force, striking boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, blockading Cuba, and waging war on Iran. It has also threatened military action against Canada and Denmark, two of the country’s long-standing allies.

American democracy, far from serving as “a light to attract strangers,” is fast becoming a cautionary tale. The second Trump administration has undermined the foundations of American power through attacks on the courts, the press, and universities. It has gleefully bulldozed through any checks on its writ. Its assault on institutions and its aggressive foreign policy are intertwined; the administration not only failed to seek congressional authorization for the war in Iran, but it also refused to even make the case to the American people before striking.

President Donald Trump has justified his aggression on the basis of the “iron laws that have always determined global power.” Morgenthau would not have recognized this as realism. He contended that “superior power gives no right, either moral or legal, to do with that power all that it is physically capable of doing.” The Trump administration, by contrast, seems to believe that to not use the power at its disposal is to waste it. Morgenthau’s verdict on Carr applies equally to Trump: he is a “Machiavelli without virtù,” playing power politics without judgment and leading his country to disaster.

Recent findings suggest that morgenthau would argue that the Trump administration misunderstands the very concept of power, which should not be equated with military might and must instead be understood as a complex psychological relationship. Real power, Morgenthau insisted, lies in the ability to influence a country through consent, not coercion. In this view, the use of force signifies the abdication of political power rather than its culmination. The Trump administration’s belligerence betrays its weakness: its acts of aggression around the world are confessions of its inability to shape events through other means.

According to recent reports, although Morgenthau grew up on the statecraft of Bismarck, he came to admire Abraham Lincoln above all others, even attempting to write a book about him toward the end of his life. Morgenthau saw in Lincoln a rare leader who was never possessed by power, instead possessing it and, ultimately, subordinating it to transcendent values. Today, just as at the height of the Vietnam War, Morgenthau would see his task as restoring morality and ethics to their rightful place and highlighting the need for power to move the world toward justice.

In a recent development, the United States has lost its purpose, and unless it rediscovers it, discrete foreign policy successes will be irrelevant. As Morgenthau wrote, if the country loses its soul, any victories are merely “footnotes to the history of the decline and fall of a once great nation.”.

DAVID SACKS is Senior Fellow for Asia Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of the forthcoming book The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power.

The AI Safety Debate Has a Human Rights Blind Spot

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
