📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

According to recent reports, AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the now-embattled target of a suspected Chinese spying operation—has been a champion of this laissez-faire approach, arguing that “the companies that are developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing,” making further regulation superfluous. In late September, the White House chimed in, imposing no latest constraints and trumpeting what President Donald Trump said would be “a tremendous self-policing aspect.”.

Yet this blizzard of pledges and manifestos seems to be doing little to reassure the public (or even key AI personnel, some of whom have resigned in alarm) that society can contain the technology’s risks. A September Quinnipiac University poll found that 74 percent of respondents held little or no trust in the leaders of AI companies. An Anthropic study published in June found that just 15 percent of Americans trust AI companies to make decisions about how the technology is developed and used.

Regulators, confronting a protean, fast-evolving technology, are facing the limits of their own competence, afraid that the wrong constraints could hamper global competitiveness and economic prosperity.

As it turns out, we are in luck, or at least potentially so. Fifteen years ago, governments unanimously endorsed a framework for addressing the human rights responsibilities of global companies. The technology industry has largely failed to incorporate these precepts into AI governance. While no panacea, it could guide a more robust, principled, and accountable approach to AI.

Industry observers note that U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan (left) and John Ruggie, special advisor to the secretary-general, arrive to attend a meeting of the Global Compact Summit at U.N. headquarters in Fresh York on June 24, 2004.Eskinder Debebe/United Nations.

Sources indicate that the modern human rights movement emerged from a ravaged world in which governments subordinated individual lives to national ambitions, ideological supremacy, and other grand designs. The U.N. Charter, signed in June 1945, affirmed the “dignity and worth of the human person.” Human beings possessed inviolable rights, irrespective of their standing, power, or capabilities.

It has been revealed that that principle acquires new relevance as machines begin to rival and surpass human capacities. Superior intelligence confers no inherent authority to govern human lives, and companies must not take steps that effectively cede such dominions. The human rights tradition offers a foundation for insisting that people retain the ability to make consequential choices, exercise independent judgment, and determine which powers may be entrusted to machines.

Recent findings suggest that the articulation of human rights initially focused on constraining governments. As multinational corporations expanded their reach, protecting individuals also required holding private enterprises accountable. Global supply chains, extractive industries, and low-wage operations in places with weak legal protections exposed serious gaps in corporate responsibility.

In 2005, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Harvard University professor and former U.N. official John Ruggie to set out the human rights responsibilities of multinational businesses. The resulting U.N. Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, unanimously endorsed by the Human Rights Council in 2011 and applicable across all industries, translated the foundational commitment to human dignity into practical expectations for how companies should operate.

Annan and Ruggie’s premise—that corporate needs and imperatives must be subordinate to the rights of humans—is one that demands reinforcement in an AI age where corporate creations show signs of challenging human dominance.

Industry observers note that ruggie’s paradigm centered on three pillars: “Protect” meant that states had a duty to shield people from abuses by businesses. A “respect” dimension identified a separate duty of companies to follow internationally recognized human rights standards, and the “remedy” element meant that people harmed by corporate activities should have redress.

Recent findings suggest that ruggie also introduced the idea of “human rights due diligence” to identify risks, prevent and mitigate harms, monitor results, and report on them. A key innovation was grounding corporate conduct in internationally recognized human rights rather than allowing individual companies to decide for themselves what ethical behavior should entail. Unlike the proclamations that we’ve seen from AI industry leaders, Ruggie’s U.N. guiding principles (UNGPs) focus on the rights of people who may be harmed by AI, rather than on the intentions or acts of companies or chatbots.

The UNGPs do not themselves create binding international law obligations for companies, although jurisdictions can enact laws to enshrine them, and some have. France, Germany, and Norway have passed laws requiring companies to identify and address human rights risks, and the European Union adopted a broad corporate due diligence directive in 2024.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”.

Sources indicate that the UNGPs spell out globally recognized rights—including privacy, freedom of expression, equality, and labor rights—and call on companies to assess how their operations and products affect them, including through actions of customers and business partners. For an AI developer, this would entail examining whether training data is obtained legitimately and how governments or businesses might use technologies for surveillance, repression, or discrimination.

The principles specify how companies should act on these assessments: embedding findings into product design, budgets, and commercial relationships as well as tracking whether safeguards work. Companies are to exert leverage over customers and partners to prevent abuses, restricting access to technology or terminating relationships when such efforts fail. They also provide a basis for insisting that decisions affecting fundamental rights remain subject to meaningful human control, with people able to understand, challenge, and reverse consequential automated actions.

Several leading legacy technology companies have made commitments explicitly invoking the UNGPs. Microsoft invoked the principles in its 2013 human rights statement, and it has issued human rights reports examining generative AI and law enforcement uses; in 2025, the company disabled specified cloud and AI services used by a unit of Israel’s Defense Ministry following revelations that its systems were being used in mass surveillance of Palestinians.

After scandals involving the platform’s complicity in acts of genocide in Myanmar and mass privacy breaches, Meta adopted an ambitious 2021 corporate human rights policy grounded in the guiding principles. Meta established an Oversight Board (of which I am a member) to scrutinize its adherence to human rights standards in content moderation. But its mandate limits probing investigation into broad issues such as privacy or effects on youth. Thus far, the Oversight Board’s jurisdiction has not been extended to AI-native products such as Muse.

Protesters hold placards warning of the human rights dangers of artificial intelligence during a rally in Amsterdam on March 8. Ana Fernandez/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, some frontier AI labs do evince awareness of human rights obligations, but they generally treat these duties as aspirational rather than obligatory. Anthropic drew on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in drafting Claude’s constitution, while a recent DeepMind Institute essay mused that responsibilities to secure AI access might “fan outwards” from governments to technology companies.

Sources indicate that the U.N. human rights office has proposed that AI developers vet high-risk customers before granting access to their models, write human rights safeguards into licenses, and enlist independent researchers and affected communities to evaluate whether safety measures actually work. Two reports to the Human Rights Council in 2025 proposed compelled disclosure of model capabilities, limitations and data provenance, and bans on mass surveillance and social scoring.

Most strikingly, one report recommends shifting the burden of proof for alleged AI-related harms from victims to companies, since the systems’ opacity will make it virtually impossible for owners to prove ill intent or even negligence.

Industry observers note that the UNGPs elaborate several further steps to make human rights adherence rigorous: They call for companies to draw on evidence from independent stakeholders to assess whether they are meeting their human rights obligations, and to make disclosures sufficient to allow outsiders to render their own judgments. AI companies could make these expectations concrete now.

Industry observers note that first, they should transform minimalist complaint and redress mechanisms in order to identify widespread harms, including privacy violations, psychological manipulation, and refusals that constrict the free flow of information. In addressing the need for grievance procedures, UNGPs recognize that patterns of complaints can expose systemic problems.

Sources indicate that consider how social media complaint systems centered on takedowns of individual pieces of content failed to adequately address wider concerns about disinformation, polarization, and youth mental health. AI companies should publish regular, detailed accounts of concerns raised about their products, including the nature and frequency of complaints, whether allegations were substantiated, and what corrective measures followed. Independent researchers, red-teamers, and civil society organizations should have formal channels to submit findings and receive substantive responses.

Second, companies should invest substantially in independent scrutiny. Human rights accountability has always depended on rigorous investigation, reporting, and advocacy by independent watchdogs. There is a necessary feedback loop between those shouldering responsibilities and those holding their feet to the fire. Governments themselves fund the U.N.’s human rights machinery, including independent experts who investigate and criticize their conduct.

FP Collections: Download must-read articles on the convergence of artificial intelligence and geopolitics. By FP Contributors.

AI companies should accept a comparable responsibility. Understanding AI demands sophisticated, labor-intensive research on a global scale; the funding to enable that will not materialize without substantial contributions from the companies themselves. They should devote a meaningful share of their growing philanthropic investments to unrestricted, multiyear grants for qualified AI safety, ethics, and human rights organizations.

Industry observers note that financial support must be accompanied by access to evidence. Independent researchers need to examine how training datasets are assembled, how models are evaluated and modified, and how external actors might manipulate the information on which AI-generated answers depend. Companies should establish broad, durable access arrangements for qualified researchers, with safeguards for privacy and security. Meta’s discontinuation of CrowdTangle in 2024 and the shuttering of the Stanford Internet Observatory demonstrated how vulnerable independent scrutiny can be to corporate decisions and political pressure.

A further commitment should concern companies’ relationships with governments, a nexus where some of AI’s gravest threats to rights may arise. Social media companies publish transparency reports on government demands for user data and content removal. Google goes further, disclosing the alleged legal grounds for takedown requests and sharing some actual notices with an independent research database.

According to recent reports, frontier AI companies’ disclosures remain rudimentary. AI developers should report when governments seek access to people’ conversations, demand restrictions or changes to model outputs, or request surveillance capabilities. Transparency should also expose the influence that companies exert on governments. The UNGPs specifically cite lobbying as an area where human rights commitments should guide corporate conduct. Microsoft and Google disclose lobbying expenditures and major trade association memberships.

It has been revealed that AI companies could go further, identifying the laws and policies that they seek to influence, the organizations that they finance, and how their advocacy comports with their human rights commitments. If they are adhering to their public professions of ethical conduct and public spiritedness, such disclosures should only reinforce their bona fides.

Industry observers note that even the existential risks associated with advanced AI fit within the framework’s logic. The Ruggie principles direct companies to prioritize preventing harms that are severe, widespread, or impossible to remedy. Risks of AI-enabled mass destruction, catastrophic infrastructure failures, or the loss of human control would demand exceptional precautions.

Sources indicate that the framework prescribes no tolerable risk threshold but specifies that decisions that could imperil entire populations cannot rest on individual corporate judgments. They require independent evidence, public accountability, and safeguards commensurate with the potential consequences.

Governments could give the Ruggie principles greater force by drawing on established approaches to product safety and corporate accountability. Automobile manufacturers must report consumer complaints, injuries, and potential defects to federal regulators, allowing patterns to emerge that may prompt investigations or recalls. AI developers could face comparable reporting requirements for harmful outputs, recurring failures, and rights violations.

In a recent development, the EU AI Act already takes notable steps in this direction, requiring developers of the most powerful models to evaluate systemic risks and report serious incidents while empowering regulators to demand information and order corrective measures or withdrawal. California’s frontier AI transparency law, which took effect in 2026, likewise mandates reporting of critical safety incidents and protects employees who raise safety concerns.

The human rights movement arose from the recognition that immense power, exercised without regard for the dignity and rights of the individual, could bring catastrophe. The companies developing artificial intelligence possess extraordinary capabilities, but they need not invent from scratch the principles by which their power should be judged and constrained. Those principles exist. The challenge is to give them force.

Industry observers note that suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

Don’t Soak the Rich

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, daniel WALDENSTROM is Professor of Economics at the Research Institute of Industrial Economics in Stockholm.
  • Weak Institutions—Not Private Fortunes—Deform Democracy.
  • According to recent reports, as private wealth continues to grow to levels never before seen in modern history, a powerful idea is taking hold in the West: the accumulation of great fortunes poses an existential threat to democracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, daniel WALDENSTROM is Professor of Economics at the Research Institute of Industrial Economics in Stockholm. He is the author of Richer and More Equal: A Newly introduced History of Wealth in the West.

Weak Institutions—Not Private Fortunes—Deform Democracy.

According to recent reports, as private wealth continues to grow to levels never before seen in modern history, a powerful idea is taking hold in the West: the accumulation of great fortunes poses an existential threat to democracy. This idea is not novel. Over a decade ago, the political scientists Jacob Hacker and Paul Pierson asserted that the rise of plutocracy has been a defining trend of American politics since the late 1970s. The economist Paul Krugman argued in 2011 that the “extreme concentration of income is incompatible with real democracy.”.

Lately, however, it has begun to gain traction in the halls of power of Western democracies. In his farewell address, former U.S. President Joe Biden argued that an “oligarchy of extreme wealth, power, and influence” was threatening “our entire democracy, our basic rights and freedoms.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez echoed the sentiment at a 2025 G-20 summit, warning that concentrated wealth “corrodes democratic institutions.”.

Some now see confiscation as the answer. After a bitter debate and over $300 million of cumulative spending by supporters and opponents, Californians rejected a statewide “billionaires’ tax” ballot measure in this week’s midterm elections. But the proposal counted among its proponents six Nobel laureates in economics, including Daron Acemoglu, Peter Diamond, and Joseph Stiglitz, who endorsed the tax in a letter framing it as “a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy.” The French economist Gabriel Zucman called the measure’s defeat “just the beginning” and vowed that though “Silicon Valley billionaires have won this battle … they will lose this war.” Several European political leaders, including the former German Green party leader Annalena Baerbock and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, have floated wealth tax proposals of their own in recent years.

Industry observers note that the risk they have identified is genuine. Democratic societies are not doing enough to prevent the superrich from unduly influencing politics. But their diagnosis—not to mention their preferred solution—is incorrect. Billionaires’ participation in politics does not in itself indicate that a democracy has been captured by moneyed interests. The strength of the political and civil institutions meant to protect against the exercise of those interests is a far more important indicator.

Sources indicate that instead of imposing wealth taxes, countries that are serious about safeguarding their political systems should take their cues from those democracies that have successfully insulated their politics from the influence of large fortunes. They should adopt transparent election laws and restraints on private campaign contributions and encourage a strong, independent media. Such measures will help make societies more democratic. Taxing wealth will simply make them poorer.

Sources indicate that arguments in favor of taxing wealth in the name of democracy often hinge on an understanding of billionaires as a monolithic bloc, committed to an agenda that runs counter to the public interest. These claims contain a kernel of truth. According to the benchmark V-Dem and Freedom House indices, the United States has indeed been in a state of democratic decline since the early 2010s. But it does not follow that billionaires as a group are responsible for this decline—or that such a unified group even exists.

Sources indicate that to empirically determine its existence, I classified the richest Americans in the 2026 Forbes 400 listing according to their traceable political donations, analyzing both their average annual giving and their total giving over the past three decades. This method is no doubt imperfect—donations can be informal or hidden and are not the only way to achieve political influence—but the pattern that emerges should nonetheless cast doubt on the idea of a single billionaire class marching on Washington.

In a recent development, the evidence reveals that roughly 30 individuals, or eight percent of U.S. billionaires in the Forbes 400, are high-level donors, giving more than $1 million each year for political purposes. Roughly half of American billionaires give on average less than $30,000 a year, 35 percent give less than $10,000, and 15 percent, or 60 of the listed billionaires, have no visible political footprint. Just 16 donors—four percent—have given more than $50 million over the last 30 years. This small minority may well plow enough money into elections to make up for the majority of billionaires with no apparent interest in politics (although if Elon Musk’s midterm outlay is any indication, even vast sums of money are no guarantee of political outcomes). But the very fact that both these groups exist suggests that the presence of the ultrawealthy alone is not necessarily responsible for American democratic decay. The weakness of the institutions meant to check their influence, on the other hand, is.

For the American billionaires who do engage in politics, federal rules and institutions make it easy to achieve disproportionate influence through large-scale private spending. Super PACs are permitted to receive unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, unions, and other political committees. The hollowing out of independent public-service media and the consolidation of private media make matters worse, allowing a small number of wealthy owners to shape the dominant narrative unchecked.

In a recent development, much of the momentum behind a wealth tax comes from the United States. But it is hardly the only country with a high proportion of superwealthy residents. Sweden and Switzerland have among the most billionaires per capita in the world, with around 4.7 and 5.0 billionaires per million inhabitants, respectively—higher than the United States’ 2.9 and dwarfing the average of 1.3 for Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries. If wealth tax proponents were correct about the relationship between extreme wealth and democratic health, one would expect both Sweden’s and Switzerland’s democracies to be in dire shape.

But in neither country has the presence of large private fortunes significantly damaged democracy. Both rank highly among liberal democracies when assessing the fairness of elections, the rule of law, checks on the executive, trust in government, and media freedom. Sweden ranks fifth in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, and Switzerland ranks eighth. As of 2025, they were tied for sixth in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index; the United States ranked 29th. According to the OECD’s 2025 trust survey, 62 percent of Swiss respondents had confidence in their national government, the highest of all countries polled. Sweden, at 42 percent, ranked 15th among the countries polled, higher than the OECD average of 40 percent and far exceeding the United States’ 27 percent, as measured by the Partnership for Public Service.

It might be tempting to point to tax policy as an explanation. Indeed, social democratic Sweden, with its 41 percent tax-to-GDP ratio as of 2024, has one of the world’s highest tax levels. Switzerland, however, maintains a tax-to-GDP ratio of roughly 27 percent, well below the OECD average of 34 percent and about even with the U.S. level of 25 percent. That these countries can support large entrepreneurial fortunes without sacrificing their democracies is in fact not the result of draconian restrictions on how those fortunes are spent in politics. Two other shared institutional features offer more compelling answers.

According to recent reports, in Sweden, political parties receive funding mainly through public structures. Private contributions are allowed, but individual donors represent a relatively small share of total party funding, and disclosure rules make all large private contributions visible. Sweden’s constitution grants citizens and journalists the right to access almost any official document. Ministers hold little direct influence over administrative agencies, allowing the agencies to operate independently of executive authority. These rules do not eliminate lobbying, but they largely prevent private money from discreetly entering and influencing the political process.

It has been revealed that switzerland’s barriers between private wealth and the levers of government, although similarly sturdy, stop money from influencing politics in slightly different ways. The country’s federal system diffuses power across 26 regional cantons and over 2,000 municipalities, and frequent regional and federal referendums give citizens veto power over legislation. Switzerland has no direct federal funding of parties and no general spending ceiling, but national disclosure rules introduced in 2022 require major campaigns and large donors to identify their financing. The country does have a wealth tax dating back to the nineteenth century, but it is administered at the canton level and its highest marginal rate is nowhere near as punitive as the California proposal. Dispersing authority and enshrining accountability over government decisions through direct democracy are far more responsible for the success of Swiss democracy.

Sources indicate that both countries also have long traditions of private journalism and independent public-service media. A mix of private outlets and public-service media, which has been shown to foster greater public trust in the news and resilience to online disinformation, prevents any single news provider from monopolizing the airwaves or suppressing information.

These institutions are not perfect, and private donations still play a role in Swedish and Swiss politics. That countries with nearly twice the number of billionaires per capita as the United States have thriving democracies should, however, give the lie to the idea that the superrich, by their mere existence, deform democracy.

The proposals currently in vogue are presented as a novel solution to the novel problem of concentrated wealth. But societies have attempted to tax wealth before. Throughout the twentieth century, many European countries imposed similarly designed taxes on household net wealth for redistributive purposes. Problems quickly emerged. Taxing individuals who rarely generated cash income and whose fortunes were thus not easily estimated outraged entrepreneurs, lowered investment, and hampered growth. In the 1970s and 1980s, governments on both the left and the right took note. They tried to discount certain business assets and exempt closely held firms from taxation to mitigate the distortions. But tinkering around these edges only caused upcoming problems of unfairness. Revenues, which at that time constituted less than half a percent of GDP across Europe, compared with total taxes that often stood at 40 percent of GDP, slumped. Ultimately, most countries scrapped the tax.

According to recent reports, many of today’s proponents are more likely to cite the threat of unprecedented fortunes to democracy than the need for redistribution as the impetus for a wealth tax. But they offer no upcoming solutions to the problems of old. Nor would a wealth tax stop billionaires from financing politics, since the wealthiest hardly need to throw the full weight of their fortunes around to wield political influence.

In a recent development, supporters might argue that the pro-democracy case for a wealth tax is much broader in scope. After all, the superrich exert influence on politics in more ways than just their donations. A wealth tax might not stop a billionaire from buying a state election, but it might stop one from, for example, buying Paramount or The Washington Post. Imperfect a solution as it is, a billionaires’ tax referendum represents a more achievable goal than amending the Constitution to wrest power from the executive.

But a wealth tax has never been an efficient fiscal tool or a substitute for substantive democratic renewal. Whatever small democratic gains it might feasibly bring would be outweighed by the threat to business ventures, capital formation, and long-term economic development it would pose. As anything more than a symbolic measure, a tax on uncertain, often illiquid values is essentially a tax on entrepreneurial risk-taking. But the case against it should not be mistaken for a broadside against all capital taxation. Governments should still seek to raise substantial revenue from taxes on the returns on capital and should set rates and brackets how they please. They must not, however, forget the crucial distinction between taxing already realized income and taxing assets that may yet generate newly introduced returns.

A better agenda to safeguard democracy against the influence of money should prioritize reforming the institutions whose weaknesses make such influence possible. Limits on campaign and party finance and more transparent disclosure of lobbying and conflicts of interest would, at the very least, make elections more difficult to buy. Increased funding for public media and stricter antitrust rules to block media mergers would create a more diverse landscape of both private and independent public-service outlets. These measures would affect just the few American billionaires who plow significant parts of their fortunes into politics, leaving the majority of the country’s wealthiest to keep doing what they do best—creating value and driving growth.

In a recent development, democracies should, of course, always fear oligarchy. They should actively work to curtail the influence of money on politics. They should not, however, confuse economic success with political capture. Countries need entrepreneurs who are willing to take risks and build wealth. Democracy will survive in an era of extraordinary fortunes not by antagonizing successful people but by making political power harder to buy.

Upcoming York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani takes a swipe at the Trump administration following multiple technical complications that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the U.S.

Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a swipe at the Trump administration Tuesday following days of tech outages sweeping the nation, saying that "the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear.".

Mamdani spoke after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country.

Industry observers note that "What I will say to New Yorkers is both an understanding of their frustration, we are speaking about New Yorkers who had made aims for months, some of them years, about going on a trip with their family or coming home from a trip with their family. And frankly, the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear," Mamdani remarked.

"And it did not leave many New Yorkers with any greater sense of confidence about our national capabilities in case of this occurring again," he continued. "And I'm looking forward to seeing Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate utilize that power to also ensure that we're delivering more answers at a national level, because what we were hearing from some of the secretaries that day was in no way confidence building.".

DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP.

The White House, when asked by Fox News Digital for comment, referred to remarks that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton made to FOX Business on Tuesday.

"We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here," Clayton said on "The Claman Countdown.".

"And we can be fairly confident in that because we know those things exist and we have been looking for them in the past," Clayton continued.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said two routers from Federal Aviation Administration facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this past Friday.

The shutdown occurred as contractor L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system.

Duffy then stated during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity" Monday that he intends to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build newly introduced architecture that is "worthy of America." The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence of a cyberattack.

According to recent reports, fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images).

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'.

In a recent development, the roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said Monday on "Hannity" that "the homeland is secure.

"Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," Mullin continued.

In a recent development, mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had issued a ground stop at all U.S. airports due to a communications problem. (Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on, to travel around Europe is often to be confronted with apocalyptic warnings. Europe and Russia are “closer now to all-out war” than at any moment since the Cuban missile crisis, Russian exile Alexander Meniukov told me at a subway station cafe in central Warsaw, Poland. “The Soviet regime was pragmatic. Putin is emotional,” he mentioned. In a hotel room in Tallinn, Estonia, I watched a news report about Romanian troops running urban combat drills on the streets of Bucharest.

European governments take seriously the prospect of war with Russia. Across the continent, defense budgets have swelled as countries rush to rearm. In 2026 alone, the European Union’s 27 member states will spend a combined 454 billion euros on their defense capacities—an 8.6 percent increase over last year’s expenditure, which marked a post-Cold War peak.

In a recent development, but as this spending intensifies, centrist lawmakers and their allies are overlooking the potential political pitfalls. This is particularly true in countries that have seemingly sacrificed other government programs on the altar of security.

Germany is a case in point. In April, Chancellor Friedrich Merz unveiled cuts to the country’s social infrastructure totaling 38.3 billion euros over the next three years. Merz has spoken often about what he sees as the necessity of streamlining Germany’s social safety net. “The welfare state that we have today can no longer be financed with what we produce in the economy,” he told a gathering of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) colleagues last year.

Meanwhile, Merz has overseen a massive increase in German military expenditure, spooked by the cumulative shock of Russia’s revanchist campaign in Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House. By 2030, Germany’s total defense outlays will hit 183.7 billion euros, one-fifth of the federal budget. Merz’s goal, widely shared across the German political spectrum, is to turn the country’s military into the most formidable fighting force in Europe by the late 2030s.

Recent findings suggest that the United Kingdom is making similar trade-offs. In June, shortly before he was ousted as prime minister, Keir Starmer published a latest “Defence Investment Plan.” If implemented, the plan will increase British government spending on core defense requirements from 2.3 percent of GDP to 2.7 percent by 2029 and then to 3.5 percent by 2035, in line with NATO mandates. This will be supported by 15 billion pounds of additional defense spending in the next four years, 7 billion pounds of which will be funded by cuts to the budgets of other departments.

Starmer acknowledged in June that the net effect of these cuts would be scrapping certain infrastructure projects and net-zero initiatives across the U.K. Notably, new Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who otherwise tends to sit to Starmer’s left, has largely accepted the proposal’s recommendations.

As tensions with Russia rise, these sums are only likely to grow. Senior European Union policymakers cast the continent’s security as a choice between social democracy and outstripping Russia’s massive defense spending. “Member states collectively spent an average 1.9 percent of GDP on defense,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs, noted in a speech in Brussels last year. “Russia is spending 9 percent. We spend billions on our schools, healthcare, and welfare, but if we don’t invest more in defense, all of this is at risk.”.

In the U.K., a cross-party coalition ranging from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to former Labour member of Parliament and NATO Secretary-General George Robertson has urged the government to implement harsher fiscal measures to fund the country’s ever-inflating defense brief. “We must cut welfare to fund our defense,” Badenoch remarked in August. “We must.”.

According to recent reports, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that such figures have lost sight of political realities. The most obvious is that across Europe, but particularly in Germany and the U.K., the far right is on the rise. According to the latest polls, Alternative for Germany (AfD) sits 10 points ahead of Merz’s CDU at the federal level. Meanwhile, Nigel Farage’s post-Brexit Reform UK party is in second, six points behind the Labour party—despite being hit by a string of financial scandals in recent months. The popularity of European far-right parties has been growing since the 2008 financial crisis; the trend is likely to accelerate with a fresh round of fiscal retrenchment.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence that cutting investment in public services bolsters support for far-right and anti-establishment movements seems more than just anecdotal. Thiemo Fetzer’s widely cited 2020 paper found a clear and “causal link between individual-or-regional-level exposure to austerity and support for Leave” in the 2016 Brexit vote, tracing the political impact of the deficit reduction policies between 2010 and 2015. At the time, both Conservative and Labour leaders argued that cuts were necessary, but they entailed massive reductions to local budgets—and an accompanying explosion in poverty rates in the regions where support for Leave was strongest.

In Germany, the Agenda 2010 reforms implemented by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) between 2003 and 2005 slashed unemployment payments and significantly raised the number of Germans in low-paid work. Part of Chancellor Gerhard Schröder’s drive to reinvigorate the economy, the reforms ultimately eroded support for the SPD and opened a political vacuum. A decade later, it has been filled by the socialist Left party and the AfD on the radical right. The AfD is the second-largest party in the Bundestag and the most popular party in the five states that make up former East Germany. Support for the SPD is at historic lows.

Both AfD co-leader Alice Weidel and Farage have been critical of Western support for Ukraine in the past and urged a more conciliatory approach toward Russia. Weidel flatly opposes further German military assistance to Ukraine and has described Kyiv’s prospective NATO membership as “completely unacceptable.” What Weidel and Farage would do if they held power is anyone’s guess. General elections in both Germany and the U.K. are due in or before 2029.

The political folly of the warfare-versus-welfare paradigm is underscored by the fact that European voters at large, exhausted by years of inflation, stagnant wages, and rising energy costs, are not keen on paying for rearmament via further attrition of their living standards. “A large majority of [Europeans] tend to disagree with any option of welfare cutbacks proposed to increase military spending,” a detailed analysis of Europe-wide polling in the Journal of European Policy concluded this year.

According to recent reports, the ongoing civil unrest in France, which started as a student-led protest against the country’s strained education system and expanded into a wider revolt over inequality and the cost of living, indicates how far working-class Europeans are prepared to go to protect what remains of postwar welfare provision. In Spain, where elections loom on Nov. 29, students and trade unionists are leading a street campaign for more affordable housing; Italy, too, has seen mass protests over rising costs. Germany and the U.K. could be next. With uniquely poor timing given the urgency of the risk posed by Russia, Europe looks increasingly distracted and divided.

Sources indicate that A further irony is that, at least in the short term, remilitarization means European states purchasing more U.S. weapons, deepening their military dependence on an unreliable partner. Under pressure from Trump, who has repeatedly dangled the threat of a U.S. withdrawal from NATO, Europe has significantly increased its volume of arms purchases from the United States. Prior to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Europe was already reliant on U.S. Patriot missiles for its security. European arms imports from the United States have since roughly doubled.

Recent findings suggest that trump’s hostility toward NATO is built on the crude belief that Europeans have been spending lavishly at the United States’ expense since the end of the Cold War. Trump has dispatched top U.S. officials, including Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to Europe in the last 18 months to hammer home the message that, from Washington’s perspective, the era of this so-called European peace dividend is over.

Yet for ordinary Europeans, the end of the Cold War didn’t necessarily generate the perks that Trump imagines. After 1991, most European countries did shrink their defense budgets. But the subsequent fiscal savings mostly weren’t spent on generous unemployment benefits or working-class wages. They were spent either on basic governmental support, such as healthcare and state pensions, or on tax cuts for corporate executives and the ultra-rich.

Sources indicate that “From the mid-1980s to 2023, corporate income tax rates fell by around half within [OECD countries],” Shahin Vallée and Joseph de Weck of the German Council for Foreign Relations wrote recently. “Social protection for the working age population has fallen across Europe since the end of the cold war.”.

Sources indicate that none of this means that Europe should not be able to defend itself against Russia, if and when a confrontation arrives; rearmament may be necessary. But it would be foolish for Europe to rearm in a way that punishes ordinary people. It is increasingly clear that the political risks of rearmament are being missed as Russian belligerence grows, the specter of U.S. isolationism intensifies, and European nerves fray.

Welfare austerity is not the only option. Governments could borrow more to bolster their defenses—or they could impose a defense tax on their richest citizens, circumventing the need to scorch front-line services. The sense of panic in Europe is real and rising, but panic does not make for good policy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, MATTHEW DUSS is Executive Vice President of the Center for International Policy. From 2017 to 2022, he served as Chief Foreign Policy Adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders.

The Imperative of Ambition in a New Congress.

It has been revealed that tuesday’s election made clear that endless wars, political corruption, and the high cost of living are three of the American public’s top concerns. They are deeply interrelated—and the new Congress must address all three. That will require a true foreign policy revolution that grapples not just with the outrages and failures of the Trump administration’s foreign policy but also with the ways in which past Democratic or Democrat-supported foreign policies have contributed to today’s crisis. There will be a temptation among some Democratic leaders, in Congress and beyond, to limit the scope or pace of change. But to find a way out of today’s crisis and move beyond the failures that have afflicted American foreign policy for the past several decades, Democrats will need to have the courage to face a hard truth: that President Donald Trump’s abuses of power and unilateral warmaking are not so much a break from Washington’s militarist mindset as they are a particularly aggressive, predatory expression of it.

Sources indicate that the incoming Democratic majority will face a national security environment in which the most severe challenges to U.S. safety and prosperity come from within. That’s why Congress should shut down the Iran war immediately but also recognize that it can make the United States more secure only if it pairs a foreign policy shift with a frontal assault on spiraling costs and political corruption. Political polarization; government corruption and dysfunction; increasing dominance of political and economic life by a small handful of mercurial oligarchs; and a president who recklessly and unilaterally debuts unauthorized military interventions while relentlessly seeking opportunities to enrich himself, his family, and his cronies—all pose more immediate danger to the safety and prosperity of the American people than does any foreign enemy.

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will have considerable power to challenge the corruption and malfeasance of the Trump administration. Control of committees and of the congressional calendar will provide the opportunity for sorely needed oversight. But although the Trump administration deserves aggressive investigation, Democrats must aim higher—and use the opportunity to articulate a genuinely compelling alternative for American foreign policy.

According to recent reports, the first and most urgent task will be ending the Iran war, a reckless and unpopular conflict that has become even less popular as Americans have felt its effects on their wallets. Congress must respond to widespread bipartisan anger among voters at Trump’s war and abuse of war powers by using all the tools it has, especially its power to cut funding. It has been encouraging to see Democrats continuing to oppose any supplemental budget request by the administration for the war. It is an area where Democrats have gotten tripped up in the past when they’ve been afraid of accusations that they don’t “support the troops” if they oppose funding for foolish, counterproductive wars. With Democrats having held firm against any additional funding for the war, those days appear to be gone. That is good.

But Democrats need to go further. They should be prepared to oppose all funding for the military, including blocking votes on the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual bill setting out the broad scope and budget for the Defense Department, in order to put an end to hostilities in Iran. In fact, not only should they be willing to withhold funding from the Pentagon, but they should also be willing to withhold funding for the entire government, and threaten another government shutdown if the bill does not prohibit any funding for Trump’s war. December 11 is the deadline for a continuing resolution to keep the government funded and operating. If ever there was a reason for Democrats to threaten to withhold their votes, stopping a blatantly illegal and globally destructive war that American voters have now resoundingly rebuked is it.

Industry observers note that democrats must also be willing to take a hard look at the continuity between Trump’s use of military violence and past uses of force by administrations of both parties, and the bipartisan support for that violence. The groundwork for the Iran war was laid by the Biden administration’s unstinting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza (as even some former administration officials have acknowledged), but also by years of U.S. refusal to impose any consequences on the Israeli government despite clear evidence of ongoing violations of human rights and international law. Trump’s strikes on alleged “narcoterrorist” drug boats in the Caribbean represent the logical evolution of long-standing treatment of the United States’ drug problem as a “war,” and of casually applying the label of “terrorist” to justify any and all measures, including execution without due process. Seeking accountability for these abuses will require acknowledging the past complicity of both Republicans and Democrats.

According to recent reports, democrats must also take on corruption, a key node connecting the country’s domestic and foreign policy crises. In doing so, they will be walking through an open door. Polls consistently show that political corruption is high on Americans’ list of concerns. According to a recent Harris poll conducted for The Guardian, “Nearly nine out of 10 Americans stated that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A mid-October CNBC All-America Economic Survey found that voters are more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices. In September, Gallup reported that “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”.

Recent findings suggest that to say that the Trump administration provides a target-rich environment for a strong anticorruption push is to commit felony understatement. Exposing foreign gifts to Trump and conflicts of interest by family members, contracts awarded to Trump’s oligarch donors and latest tech buddies, and the selling of pardons, as well as restoring enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and related task forces, should all be part of the strategy. Democrats should drill down into Trump’s wildly corrupt “Board of Peace” for Gaza, which U.S. Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, rightly referred to as a “global slush fund.” The obvious conflicts of interests of Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also demand investigation.

The good news is that effective anticorruption does not necessarily require latest legislation; it merely requires that existing legislation be enforced. An August 2025 essay in Foreign Affairs, co-authored with my colleagues Casey Michel and Trevor Sutton, laid out a more expansive case for Democrats putting anticorruption at the center of their foreign policy platform. (A recent essay by Casey Michel lays out a more detailed agenda for the new Congress.).

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the most crucial step toward tackling corruption will be reforming the campaign finance system. The United States is an outlier among developed democracies in that its system of campaign finance allows for what is essentially legalized bribery. Legislators speak openly about campaign contributors expecting “returns on investment” for their political donations. This is an outrage. In recent years, foreign actors have increasingly begun bankrolling American legislators, taking advantage of massive loopholes in campaign finance laws and the Federal Election Commission’s lack of enforcement.

Confronting this will be no small task. At a minimum, Congress must move to legislate a response to the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, which effectively greenlighted bottomless campaign funding from American corporations. It must also reform the Federal Election Commission, providing the body with much-needed resources to investigate campaign finance crimes and restoring the practice of allowing congressional appointments to the commission, which has become little more than an appendage of the executive branch.

All of the above steps must be connected to the top concern among American voters at this moment—the high cost of living. Democrats have disagreements in several policy areas, particularly in foreign policy. Their coalition is diverse. But there is consensus around addressing Americans’ material needs urgently and aggressively. Such an approach would confront Trump’s reckless use of tariffs (while recognizing that the neoliberal taboo on tariffs is a thing of the past), rising gas prices because of the Iran war, the need to restore the global minimum tax, the threat of job losses to AI, and the increased power of tech oligarchs over Americans’ economic and political lives, including on foreign policy, as Elon Musk’s restriction of Ukraine’s Starlink connection demonstrated. The approach should involve a mix of tactics, including hearings, oversight investigations, and legislative proposals.

Sources indicate that many of these efforts may not produce newly introduced laws in the next two years. But they could become the backbone of a winning agenda for Congress and for a Democratic administration in 2029. Most important, they would represent a step toward the forging of a new American political consensus on which a new and durable foreign policy can be built.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” stated Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”.

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”.

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” stated Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”.

In February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades. The government tapped the military to protect strategic mining areas, extended mining contracts from 25 years to as long as 40 years, and replaced its rigorous environmental licensing system with an authorization process that allows projects deemed low impact to skip environmental review and citizen consultation.

Industry observers note that noboa argued that mining is Ecuador’s ticket out of poverty. The country is home to an estimated $220 billion of untapped mineral wealth—mostly gold, copper, and silver, according to the World Bank. But Ecuador has geochemically mapped just 30 percent of its territory, compared to 77 and 85 percent in neighboring Peru and Colombia, respectively. Ecuador’s two existing industrial mines didn’t begin large-scale extraction until 2019.

It has been revealed that that is partly due to legal protections: Ecuador enshrined the rights of nature in its 2008 constitution, which requires environmental consultations and consent from affected Indigenous groups before major mining projects can begin. The constitution also allows communities to force referendums that can halt extractive projects.

Recent findings suggest that noboa wants to change that. His government has framed rolling back regulations and militarizing the sector as the path to dismantling illegal mining and bringing sustainable investment to Ecuador. Economists and security experts doubt that his policies can deliver on either front.

“There are potentially massive benefits to [mining]. But there are massive costs, too,” said Monica DeBolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. If your objective is to have the benefits outweigh the costs, she said, “it all boils down to governance.” That has been a major concern for Noboa, who observers have accused of executive overreach.

Noboa was elected president in 2023. He kicked off his pro-mining agenda the next year, attending the world’s largest mining convention in Canada and leading a delegation that secured investment commitments in Ecuador worth nearly $5 billion from companies in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

After the visit, Noboa used an executive decree to concentrate mining, environmental, security, and financial powers into a single presidential committee. He followed up in 2025 by reopening Ecuador’s mining registry for the first time in seven years and absorbing the Environment Ministry into the Energy and Mining Ministry.

That October, Noboa signed another presidential decree, this time barring nonprofits from “obstruction or interfering” with legally authorized mining projects and requiring them to seek ministry approval for any social programs. He ended the year with yet another decree, handing Ecuador’s mining regulator broad control over concessions and royalties, making it easier for mining companies to move into fresh areas.

It has been revealed that the last decree laid the groundwork for the February overhaul: a sweeping mining reform that loosened environmental licensing, authorized military control of private concessions, and set the stage for a U.S.-backed crackdown on illegal mining. Throughout his time in office, Noboa has also invoked his fight against organized crime to declare states of emergency that curb civil liberties and expand military control over mining provinces.

“No other government—including my own—has ever pushed mining so aggressively,” stated Fernando Benalcázar, Ecuador’s former vice minister of mines, who was in office when Ecuador’s two existing large-scale mines—Fruta del Norte and Mirador—came online. Both are in the Amazon rainforest, near the border with Peru. Under Noboa, another six major projects are in various stages of development.

It has been revealed that ecuador’s mining sector generated a total of nearly 12,000 direct jobs through the fourth quarter of 2025, and some estimates project that the industry may create another 460,000 direct and indirect positions by 2030. Minerals, which produced a record $4.16 billion in export revenues in 2025, now fall just behind Ecuador’s other top non-oil exports: cacao, bananas, and shrimp.

Recent findings suggest that but Noboa’s determination to rewrite Ecuador’s mining landscape has put him on a collision course with the constitutional order. The political opposition has argued that Noboa’s policies have relied on sidelining regulatory institutions and local communities. In the words of legislator Verónica Iñiguez, the president’s agenda “put the rat in charge of guarding the cheese.”.

It has been revealed that noboa’s mining decrees have not yet faced direct judicial challenges, but Ecuador’s top court has curbed many of his emergency declarations. It has also agreed to hear a challenge to the February mining law brought by Indigenous and community organizations. The plaintiffs argue that the government violated the constitution by failing to consult Indigenous communities, authorizing military activity in ancestral territories, and weakening environmental safeguards.

Sources indicate that although they might promote investment in the short term, aggressive tactics like Noboa’s can backfire in the long term, according to analysts. When top-down mining policy meets resistance in the form of legal setbacks and popular opposition, it creates uncertainty that spooks investors.

“If there’s one thing that investors hate, that one thing is uncertainty,” DeBolle mentioned. “[Policies] at loggerheads with the country’s constitution—that’s a recipe for uncertainty.” The World Bank likewise emphasizes that strong, transparent, and independent government institutions are critical for resource-rich countries to capture and sustain the benefits of mining.

According to recent reports, mounting opposition has already forced Noboa’s government to backtrack on projects that it rushed through. In 2025, the government issued a license for Dundee Precious Metals’ Loma Larga gold-silver-copper mine, despite local resistance and environmental concerns. The site rests atop a fragile ecosystem and a crucial water source, and communities repeatedly voted against mining there. After the rushed approval, local authorities and residents mobilized—filing lawsuits, launching media campaigns, and organizing a “March for Water” with more than 100,000 participants.

Recent findings suggest that noboa’s office declared in late September that it would revoke the mine’s license. The environmental ministry did so a week later.

Industry observers note that noboa’s push to fast-track mining permissions isn’t just a bid for investment. Paired with military operations against illegal mines, the government also casts approved mining projects as a security tool to weaken organized crime groups, which have pushed into the illegal mining sector over the past decade. By 2024, illegal mining was estimated to generate up to $1 billion a year for criminal groups in Ecuador.

In March, Noboa declared that Ecuador and the United States would increase their cooperation to fight illegal mining and drug trafficking. By October, Ecuador’s military said that it had destroyed more than 1,000 illegal mining camps so far this year. Authorities have not released official casualty figures, but according to local reporting, there have been at least three deaths and many more injuries in these operations.

Luis Córdova Alarcón, who heads a program on conflict and violence at the Central University of Ecuador, said that the logic at the heart of Noboa’s policy is backward. “Legal mining isn’t the opposite of illegal mining. It is its partner in crime,” he said.

According to recent reports, córdova, who described the militarized approach as a “smokescreen,” pointed to illegal extraction within legally granted mining concessions, including arrangements in which concession holders rent access to illegal miners. He also highlighted the formal sector’s role in laundering illegal gold and the  direct involvement of corrupt figures in the criminal economy. His conclusions are backed by the United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime (UNODC), which recently published a report concluding that legally registered corporations can “become involved in illegal mining in different ways,” including infiltration by organized crime groups.

Industry observers note that multinational companies bring their own risks, including corruption, tax evasion, weak ownership transparency, and community conflict, remarked Julia Yansura, the program director for environmental crime and illicit finance at the FACT Coalition, a Washington-based financial-transparency advocacy group. “I think some governments can’t accept or don’t see risk with these massive mining companies. It’s like they’re totally blind to it,” she said.

It has been revealed that easing regulation may open the door to more opaque foreign companies and weaker safeguards, according to Yansura. Militarized crackdowns ignore this sort of illegal mining, targeting small-scale and informal operations tied to organized crime. Yet even when it comes to informal small-scale mining, research has shown militarized approaches to be ineffective in the long run.

It has been revealed that authorities “blow up machinery, harass local people, and then leave,” Yansura mentioned. “That doesn’t actually solve the problem.” In fact, such operations can push miners deeper into illegality, undermine trust in public authorities, and fuel conflict and corruption.

For governments to curb illegal mining and undermine organized crime, UNODC recommends increasing regulation rather than relaxing it, holding big corporations criminally responsible for participating in or facilitating illegal mining activity, and empowering affected communities through democratic engagement.

Recent findings suggest that noboa is failing on that last front. His mining policies are part of a broader centralization of power that has weakened Ecuador’s democracy. Under the guise of combating illegal mining, Noboa’s administration has pushed through legislation that expands his emergency powers, reduces restrictions on using lethal force against civilians, increases state surveillance, centralizes executive control over protected areas, and targets financing for environmental nongovernmental organization.

Recent findings suggest that indigenous groups, human rights advocates, and environmental defenders say that Noboa’s administration has used these laws to go after individuals who oppose his mining policies. They point to recent criminal charges against water defenders, the violent police dispersal of anti-mining protests in the capital of Quito in February, and the conviction of at least 15 anti-mining protesters on criminal charges throughout the course of this year.

“Quite simply, what the Ecuadorian government is doing is rolling back rights and eroding the institutions meant to protect them,” Iñiguez said.

Recent findings suggest that in August 2025, when Ecuador’s highest court challenged the constitutionality of some of the new laws, Noboa led a march on the court, and senior members of his administration called judges “enemies of the citizenry,” alarming observers. He defended the suspended security measures and his efforts to pressure Ecuadorian institutions as necessary to combat criminal gangs, telling a crowd at the march that “[w]e are here to pursue justice and peace.”.

A month later, when Ecuador’s powerful Indigenous movement CONAIE declared a nationwide strike triggered by the end of fuel subsidies, Noboa deployed the military to break up roadblocks, resulting in at least three civilian deaths, and vowed to prosecute protest leaders for terrorism under a new statute. In October 2025, CONAIE called off the strike, citing fear of government violence.

Noboa’s aggressive approach initially appeared popular with a public preoccupied with crime. But that changed on Nov. 16, 2025, when Ecuadorians went to the polls to vote in a national referendum. In a surprise upset, Noboa lost all four questions that would have further concentrated power in the executive. The biggest rebuke was to his proposal to convene a constituent assembly: Voters rejected rewriting Ecuador’s environmentally protective constitution.

Recent findings suggest that continuing to push through mining policy at odds with Ecuador’s constitution may turn out to be Noboa’s Achilles heel. Polling demonstrated a sharp decline in the president’s approval ratings in the first half of this year compared to 2025. “The decline stems directly from his failure to respect the mandate of the ballot box,” Iñiguez remarked.

#30359. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
