China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security.
  • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
  • Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

And America Should Be Taking Notes.

Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining users across the developing world.

If the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

Recent findings suggest that the Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom revealed it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

China responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

That basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

In a recent development, to win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

WAICO has quickly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

Xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in Newly introduced Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

It has been revealed that much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or company can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

Recent findings suggest that china’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

In a recent development, the Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

This September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security glitch, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

Xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

This record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

Sources indicate that but Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

Industry observers note that the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

According to recent reports, these conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of new Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

More broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

Much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

It has been revealed that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

China, however, may have already beaten Trump to the punch.

Right out of the gate, Chinese President Xi Jinping has signaled that his administration is willing to act as a counterweight to the White House’s increasingly provocative trade policies. On Tuesday, Beijing agreed to cut duties on a swath of Canadian exports, amounting to roughly $280 million in tariff relief. In exchange, Ottawa promised to extend remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by another two years.

“Stronger communication and cooperation between China and Canada will benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world,” Xi told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during talks in Shenzhen, China. This was their third meeting since Carney took power in 2025, and it marked Ottawa’s continued efforts to diversify its trade away from Washington.

Sources indicate that china also pledged on Tuesday to provide Peru with $22.5 million in aid to address what is expected to be the devastating fallout of this year’s El Niño. Lima applauded the measure, with President Keiko Fujimori stressing that “China is very important to us because it is our ​principal trading partner.”.

Peru is one of the many places in Latin America where Beijing and Washington have competed for influence. Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department disclosed that it has committed $4.5 million to help Peru modernize its main port at Callao, in a move seen as a direct counter to a Chinese-controlled megaport less than 50 miles away that opened in 2024.

According to recent reports, perhaps most notably, though, is China’s potential openness to converse with Japan. A war of words over Taiwan, coupled with Beijing’s rare-earth export controls, has plagued Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s tenure. However, during Tuesday’s ASEAN gathering in Manila, Takaichi shook hands with Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu. Although few words were exchanged, the fact that such an interaction occurred has raised hopes that Takaichi’s upcoming trip to Shenzhen may be more cordial than previously anticipated.

Sources indicate that yet Beijing’s biggest days may still be to come. On Wednesday, Xi will host Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks on nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. With Trump at his weakest point to date (entering his lame-duck term after sweeping midterm losses and a Nvidia spy scandal), experts anticipate that Xi will aim to capitalize on Trump’s rocky footing.

Sources indicate that “Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency,” FP columnist Howard W. French argued.

Dirty bomb threat? Iran is actively planning for potential strikes on U.S. soil, seven U.S. officials told CNN on Tuesday. Whether Tehran will or even can execute such an attack is unclear, and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis has insisted that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Still, even the possibility of such an assault signals growing alarm that a peaceful end to the Iran war may be out of reach.

CNN reported that, according to U.S. intelligence, Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. Sources told CNN that this is not an indicator of an imminent attack but rather is one of several options that Iran may be exploring. Iranian officials, however, denied the report, with chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calling it “false flags” and “war mongering.”.

According to recent reports, experts, meanwhile, insist that Tehran may not have the capabilities or the desire to carry out such a plot. “An Iranian dirty bomb in Washington would be very hard to pull off,” retired U.S. Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN. “They’d have to move uranium halfway around the world and have a team in place to set it off. I don’t think they’ll do it. The U.S. response would be overwhelming.”.

According to recent reports, trump expressed a similar notion on Tuesday. When asked about the CNN article, the U.S. president told reporters that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” were it to attack the United States homeland.

Recent findings suggest that crosshairs on Crimean bridge. Ukrainian forces introduced a second strike on Tuesday at a strategic bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever,’” Ukraine’s military command stated in a statement. “Now, part of the structure lies in the water.” The attack marked the second consecutive assault on the critical crossing in just two days.

Industry observers note that the Kerch Strait Bridge—often highlighted as one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects—is the only rail crossing between Russia and the Crimean territory. Moscow has repeatedly used the 12-mile road to transport military and civilian supplies to its troops as well as to exert control over Ukraine’s southern coast; the Kerch Strait acts as a chokepoint for naval access from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. In recent years, the route has also become a symbol of Russia’s yearslong occupation.

According to recent reports, ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized this week’s attacks on the bridge as the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes. Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed on Tuesday that the assault on Kerch Strait Bridge occurred in tandem with a massive Ukrainian drone operation; Moscow claimed to have intercepted 1,441 drones across 22 regions on Tuesday in one of Kyiv’s biggest such attacks yet.

What is Belgrade’s future? Hundreds of people gathered outside Serbia’s National Assembly on Tuesday to cheer on the country’s latest parliament, the first since the ouster of President Aleksandar Vucic. Led by the grassroots Student List movement, the inaugural session kicked off what is expected to be the long process of forming a government.

Nearly two years of student-led protests against one of Europe’s most staunchly populist regimes culminated in the opposition’s sweeping victory in parliamentary elections last month. Student List lawmakers dominated in the polls, winning 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly compared to the Vucic-led Serbian Progressive Party’s 103 seats. Vucic initially blamed foreign interference for his loss, without citing evidence, despite international observers noting that his party held an unfair advantage.

Now begins the difficult task of governing a country that has been led by Vucic for the past 14 years. On Tuesday, the Student List was expected to nominate university professor Aleksandar Cupic to be the country’s fresh parliamentary speaker. After that, the grassroots movement will still have to choose a prime minister and hold a snap presidential election; the deadline for the latter expires at the end of this year.

The end of Pope Leo XIV’s 12-day Latin America tour wrapped up this week with a painful surprise. While traveling in the popemobile before his final Mass in Peru on Monday, Leo was struck in the eye by a flying rosary. It is unclear who threw the prayer beads, as worshippers often toss gifts at the pope, who is known for his (usually) quick reflexes.

Sources indicate that however, Leo has already shaken off the incident. “The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart—or maybe in your eye—but that mark the life of someone,” Leo stated on Tuesday.

Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the One Significant Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
  • A residential solar project in Upcoming York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
  • According to recent reports, after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the One Significant Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is right now available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

A residential solar project in Upcoming York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

According to recent reports, after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial organization, and not the homeowner.

In a recent development, some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central Fresh York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

“We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” mentioned Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

Industry observers note that TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

Industry observers note that these are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

Selling residential solar in 2026.

In a recent development, rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the manufacturer’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright remarked he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

It has been revealed that wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

“I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my organization and the industry more than the customer,” Wright remarked. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright remarked.

According to recent reports, NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York. Nickels noted that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

Sources indicate that “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels said. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

According to recent reports, some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states at the moment have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

According to recent reports, while traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels stated.

#30340. Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3534 w)

Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that STEPHEN E.
  • EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
  • Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

And Now He Needs a Fresh Strategy.

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump revealed that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

Sources indicate that trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

If leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

Sources indicate that for a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

Recent findings suggest that although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

Since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

In a recent development, even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the upcoming memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

Still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

Recent findings suggest that russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most notable partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the issue. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s upcoming approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

It has been revealed that whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

Sources indicate that the Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

Although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a latest opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

Sources indicate that three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same glitch that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

One possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

Kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

According to recent reports, in the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

Industry observers note that regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

Recent findings suggest that finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

If North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a new campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

Industry observers note that beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as important: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

Recent findings suggest that even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

In a recent development, any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

In a recent development, despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

Industry observers note that trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

In a recent development, the bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the problem, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

In a recent development, growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

Sources indicate that but this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

Iran Is Heading for a Swiss-Cheese Solution

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside.
  • It has been revealed that pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms.
  • President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

It has been revealed that pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a fresh government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

Pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

In a recent development, second, in two months’ time, Trump’s maneuverability will be eclipsed by a Democratic Congress that can defund the war. Third, though U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment attempt last week, his political future still hangs by a thread.

Even if the risk of war declines, this does not guarantee a greater likelihood of a deal. Key obstacles—including Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, the future of its enrichment program, a regional cease-fire, sanctions relief, and the political cost for Trump—make both reaching and maintaining an agreement challenging.

According to recent reports, the most likely scenario may turn out to be neither war nor peace, yet something altogether different from the economic blockade “middle path” that Trump chose earlier. In this scenario, Trump’s economic warfare and blockade would end up little more than words on paper. Trump would declare victory, reject both war and peace, withdraw the U.S. military, step away from the table, and insist that the blockade and sanctions remain in place while quietly allowing them to fade into irrelevance.

This would set in motion a gradual loosening of the blockade, with sanctions enforcement quietly eroding. Bit by bit, Asian and Middle Eastern countries would ramp up trade and investment in Iran, far surpassing current levels. Out of this slow transformation, a delicate upcoming equilibrium would take shape: Sanctions enforcement would remain just robust enough for the United States to insist the system is intact, yet lax enough to persuade Tehran not to upset the emerging status quo.

This Swiss-cheese scenario is the only walk-away option that could work. If Trump truly keeps the blockade and sanctions in place, then the United States and Iran would be locked in a relentless standoff, always teetering on the edge of conflict, just as they are now. This fragile balance would inevitably tip into another war, completely undermining the whole point of walking away.

According to recent reports, to be clear, the Swiss-cheese scenario is suboptimal compared with a peace deal. A peace deal that would end 47 years of enmity, uphold nonproliferation goals, open the Iranian economy to U.S. companies, and stabilize the region would far better serve U.S. interests. But the walk-away option carries the benefit, from Trump’s perspective, of avoiding an agreement that would manifest the failure of his war, as the Islamabad Memorandum did in the view of its critics. He will find it attractive because his focus is no longer on how much he can get, but how much he can avoid giving.

It has been revealed that indeed, the Swiss-cheese option guarantees that, while none of the sides walks away with a complete victory, everyone sidesteps their worst nightmare. Trump escapes both a humiliating compromise and the quagmire of another needless war. Tehran, in turn, dodges the devastation that a joint U,S. and Israeli assault on its vital infrastructure and energy lifelines would unleash. And given the shift in favor of nuclear weapons among the Iranian public, Iranian decision-makers may also welcome de facto partial sanctions relief without having to give up their stockpile of enriched uranium or give other nuclear concessions.

It has been revealed that even Israel might breathe easier, since its worst fear—a U.S.-Iran diplomatic breakthrough that could see old enemies reconcile—remains off the table, while the possibility of a future U.S.-Iran conflict still lingers. Israeli leaders will certainly view any loosening of the sanctions pressure as a loss, but it is still superior to a deal that undoes the sanctions architecture altogether. Moreover, Israel may calculate that the scenario still offers plenty of opportunities to tighten the sanctions or even escalate matters toward war.

In short, it’s neither side’s worst option, and everyone’s least-costly scenario.

And while Israel may still hope for chances to escalate, the Swiss-cheese scenario could turn out to be unexpectedly resilient, even as it leaves the U.S.-Iran conflict unresolved. Should this uneasy balance persist until 2029, the next U.S. president will stand at a crossroads: reignite tensions in pursuit of a better deal or quietly embrace the status quo and turn attention to the many other pressing crises on the United States’ plate. To most presidents, this will be a rather simple choice.

According to recent reports, given Trump’s refusal to admit defeat, his dread of looking like a loser, his allergy to tangled diplomacy, his fixation on eclipsing former U.S. President Barak Obama’s Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, and Iran’s refusal to offer him an ego-saving escape, Trump may ultimately declare a false victory and settle for the Swiss-cheese walk-away—not because it’s the smarter move but because it’s the cheapest way out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to defend its budget as President Donald Trump and other former defendants seek nearly $17 million in legal-fee reimbursements, but an appeals judge noted the office was not entitled to due process.

A Georgia appellate judge pressed Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis’ office Tuesday as it pushed for permission to fight millions in legal-fee requests from President Donald Trump and other former defendants in her collapsed election interference case.

Before a three-judge panel, Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to protect its budget from payments stemming from a prosecution she and her office were disqualified from handling in December 2024.

Sources indicate that "What process are you entitled to? You’re the government. Due process doesn’t apply to you," Judge J. Wade Padgett told Donald Wakeford, a chief senior assistant district attorney representing Willis’ office.

Recent findings suggest that trump and other former defendants are seeking nearly $17 million under a Georgia law passed last year, with Trump alone requesting more than $6 million. The law allows defendants to recover legal fees if their prosecutor is removed for improper conduct and their charges are later dismissed.

MIKE DAVIS: CALIFORNIA'S HIGHEST COURT DISGRACES ITSELF BY UPHOLDING DISBARMENT OF JOHN EASTMAN.

President Donald Trump (left) and Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (right). Prosecutors in Georgia are seeking more time to appoint a latest attorney after Willis was disqualified from handling Trump’s election interference case. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Alex Slitz-Pool/Getty Images).

Tuesday’s hearing focused on whether Willis’ office could participate in challenging those requests.

The state is represented in the reimbursement fight by Pete Skandalakis, executive director of the Prosecuting Attorneys’ Council of Georgia, who took over after Willis’ disqualification and moved to dismiss the charges in November 2025.

Recent findings suggest that willis’ office argued he cannot adequately protect its financial interests because his own decision to drop the case opened the door to the reimbursement requests. Wakeford also argued that Skandalakis’ authority in the case ended when the prosecution did.

"This statute has created a mess and that is no secret," Wakeford stated of the new Georgia law allowing defendants to seek reimbursement for their legal fees.

The judges pressed him on whether Willis’ disqualification still bars her office from participating.

MIKE DAVIS: DISGRACED GEORGIA JUDGE MUST LEAVE THE BENCH OVER SEX SCANDAL.

Sources indicate that special prosecutors Nathan Wade, left, and Daysha Young talk amongst themselves during a hearing on the Georgia election interference case, on March 1, 2024, in Atlanta, Georgia. (Alex Slitz / Getty Images).

"So let’s talk about the elephant in the room then," Padgett said, pointing to the court’s earlier ruling declaring the district attorney wholly disqualified.

"The criminal prosecution has ended," Wakeford responded, arguing that the fee dispute is a separate matter.

"Is the disqualification over? Is she no longer wholly disqualified?" Judge Ken Hodges asked.

Wakeford noted that Willis’ disqualification applied to the criminal prosecution, arguing it did not bar her office from participating in the separate legal-fee dispute.

But the panel also questioned whether that finding satisfies the fresh law’s requirements for reimbursement.

CALIFORNIA HIGH COURT ORDERS DISBARRING OF FORMER TRUMP ATTORNEY OVER EFFORT TO DISPUTE 2020 ELECTION RESULTS.

Fani Willis, Fulton County District Attorney, at the Fulton County Courthouse in Atlanta, Georgia, US, on Friday, March 1, 2024. (Alex Slitz/AP/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"The trial judge found an appearance of impropriety and found that actual misconduct had not been established," Padgett noted.

Willis and her office were removed from the case after an appeals court found that her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special prosecutor she appointed, created an appearance of impropriety.

In March, Fulton County Superior Court Judge Scott McAfee denied Willis’ request to intervene, finding that Skandalakis could adequately represent her office’s interests. Her office is asking the appeals court to overturn that decision.
