The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • According to recent reports, in just a few days’ time, U.S.
  • These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

According to recent reports, in just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm strategy has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

According to recent reports, if he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core problems that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

It has been revealed that yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

Sources indicate that if they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious initiative for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a blueprint for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a newly introduced round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

Sources indicate that A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

According to recent reports, xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

According to recent reports, trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these complications.

Sources indicate that trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

According to recent reports, neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

Industry observers note that as a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

In a recent development, beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, Newly introduced START, ended in February. There are at the moment no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

According to recent reports, realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Industry observers note that trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a newly introduced Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a latest era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani revealed more than $500 million in luxury second-home tax billings despite thousands of property exemptions and ongoing legal challenges.

New York City has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million under Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial pied-à-terre tax, even as the number of homeowners receiving bills fell far below initial estimates.

"We've billed more than $500 million to owners of second homes worth more than $5 million," Mamdani wrote on X Tuesday.

"That's half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all Latest Yorkers," he continued.

According to information provided by city officials, the Latest York City Department of Finance mailed approximately 7,500 tax bills — a sizable drop from the roughly 17,000 initial notices sent to property owners over the summer.

APPEALS COURT HANDS MAMDANI LEGAL WIN ON NYC LUXURY SECOND-HOME TAX.

Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to reporters' questions during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images).

Officials also said roughly 8,900 exemption applications were granted, while approximately 1,600 extension applications were denied.

The surcharge is a key part of the mayor's agenda to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and help close the city's budget gap.

Despite the smaller number of bills, the city stated the total amount billed exceeded the $500 million target previously outlined by Gov. Kathy Hochul earlier this year.

However, officials did not immediately provide a breakdown showing how the total was calculated across the approximately 7,500 properties.

"As Mayor Mamdani has said before, owning a second home worth over 5 million dollars should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable," Julia Agos, a spokesperson for the Department of Finance, said in a statement to Fox News Digital."The Department of Finance will continue to implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone," Agos added.

The tax is assessed on a sliding scale based on property values, meaning owners of more expensive homes can face higher charges.

JIM GAFFIGAN, UPCOMING YORK LAWMAKERS PUSH GOV HOCHUL TO AXE 'UNNECESSARY TAX' HITTING COMEDY CLUBS.

It has been revealed that newly introduced York City luxury residential towers and Mayor Zohran Mamdani amid a legal battle over the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images/Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images).

In an April report, the New York City comptroller's office estimated that a version of the tax could generate approximately $500 million from more than 11,200 properties before accounting for exemptions and changes in homeowner behavior.

After accounting for those factors, however, the report projected that revenue could fall to between roughly $340 million and $380 million.

Still, Mamdani has continued to express confidence in the surcharge's revenue potential, telling reporters last week, "We continue to be confident in its ability to raise half a billion dollars per year.".

The surcharge, approved by the Newly introduced York state Legislature in May, applies to qualifying luxury second homes in New York City, including certain one- to three-family properties valued at $5 million or more and condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more.

MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY FRESH YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'.

In a recent development, fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that the city has billed more than $500 million under its luxury second-home tax, despite issuing fewer bills than the number of initial notices sent to property owners. (Lev Radin/Sipa USA).

Property owners who qualify for exemptions are not subject to the surcharge.

Tuesday's announcement comes after a state appeals court handed Mamdani a legal victory earlier this month, unanimously dismissing a lawsuit challenging the rollout of the surcharge.

The court found that the homeowners who brought the lawsuit lacked legal standing, overturning a lower court ruling that had ordered the city to restart implementation.

However, the tax continues to face separate legal challenges, including questions about its constitutionality.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
  • The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • It has been revealed that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

Sources indicate that in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

It has been revealed that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

In a recent development, beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

While Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. Fresh York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Recent findings suggest that wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

In a recent development, the appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that alaska Democratic Sen.-elect Mary Peltola reacted Tuesday to defeating Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, saying "we are going to put Alaska first." (X/Mary Peltola).

It has been revealed that democrats flipped a ninth GOP-held Senate seat in the 2026 midterm elections, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.

It has been revealed that peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate.

"Alaskans have voted for change, and I'm so honored to be your next U.S. senator," Peltola said in a social media video released after The Associated Press called the race Tuesday two weeks after Election Day. "Together, we're gonna put an end to the era of self-serving politicians lining their own pockets at your expense. And together, we are going to put Alaska first.".

Peltola defeated Sullivan with 50.1% of the vote, avoiding a ranked-choice vote count.

The contest emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Republicans defending a seat in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, and Democrats eyeing a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory.

The controversy deepened just days before Election Day when The Fresh York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had participated in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name.

It has been revealed that alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson).

Recent findings suggest that according to the Times, text messages and interviews revealed a broader operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," aimed at recruiting candidates who could siphon votes from Sullivan. The effort reportedly involved the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and included discussions about establishing a upcoming right-wing political party.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign, while the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) also rejected allegations of participation. The revelations prompted Republican Gov. Michael Dunleavy to order an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law.

The Cook Political Report rated the contest a toss-up, reflecting the unusually competitive environment in a state that has generally favored Republicans in federal elections.

Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election to succeed the late Republican Rep. Don Young.

GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING.

Industry observers note that sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Getty Images).

She defeated former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin in that contest before winning a full term later that year. Peltola subsequently lost her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III, setting the stage for her Senate campaign.

Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, first won his Senate seat in 2014 by defeating Democratic incumbent Mark Begich, Nick's uncle. He secured reelection in 2020 and sought a third term emphasizing his experience, national security and Alaska's energy interests.

It has been revealed that the 2026 race also featured an unusual ballot controversy involving Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who shared nearly the same name as the Republican incumbent.

Alaska election officials initially moved to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot amid allegations that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon support from the senator. The candidate denied wrongdoing, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot. The DOJ sued in October to mitigate any "misleading" impact of the newcomer Sullivan.

COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’.

The controversy added another complication to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.

Under the system, a candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes wins outright. Otherwise, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated, and ballots are redistributed according to voters' next available preferences until a winner emerges.

Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, is seen against the Chugach Range. (Getty Images/Getty Images).

Peltola had previously benefited from the system during her 2022 congressional victories, when ranked-choice tabulation helped determine the outcomes of races featuring multiple Republican opponents.

The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • According to recent reports, at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

According to recent reports, at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

Sources indicate that in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

Sources indicate that at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

In a recent development, international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

According to recent reports, A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

The integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

Recent findings suggest that together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will quickly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

Sources indicate that in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

But these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

War also creates latest dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

It has been revealed that finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to fresh waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

In a recent development, spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

In a recent development, from day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Sources indicate that countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

It has been revealed that investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

Sources indicate that yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

According to recent reports, some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Recent findings suggest that other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

Sources indicate that the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

Industry observers note that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

According to recent reports, the first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An update to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly vital, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The upcoming seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats presently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

It has been revealed that permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

According to recent reports, A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

It has been revealed that another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Recent findings suggest that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

Sources indicate that technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

Sources indicate that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

According to recent reports, proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a newly introduced UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing rapidly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

Recent findings suggest that this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, rolled out with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

Industry observers note that A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

It has been revealed that white House counsel Will Scharf joins 'Fox News Sunday' to address incoming Democratic investigations targeting the Trump administration. Scharf warns that the Department of Justice will push back aggressively if lawmakers use their oversight powers to threaten or intimidate administration staffers.

The likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee is officially taking the first steps to launch a wide array of investigations before Democrats take control in the new Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is sending document preservation letters to 12 figures in President Donald Trump's orbit on Wednesday morning, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

House Oversight Committee Democrats are looking to investigate the Trump family's business deals, alleged misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, they said in a release.

Garcia remarked the probes "will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans.".

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS.

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry Golf Club on July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images).

The California Democrat is all but guaranteed to hold the Oversight gavel in the next Congress and has already signaled that he intends to kick off the new year with an aggressive investigation schedule.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH.

His committee will also be key to any potential impeachment efforts House Democrats take on in the next term.

In a recent development, other investigatory targets include former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," letters to the president's two eldest sons read.

"While the Trump Administration’s failed policies have made life increasingly unaffordable for the public, you have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people.".

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House Office Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images).

The letter to Miller reads in part, "Oversight Democrats have heard directly from the victims of the lawless conduct of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign and from whistleblowers appalled by agency behavior. There must be accountability for those responsible for orchestrating, carrying out, and covering up these abuses, at all levels of the agency.".

DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS.

Democrats have positioned their investigative efforts as accountability measures long-sought by the American public. But Republicans have argued that it highlights Democrats are more interested in political retribution than working on solutions to lower concerns like the high cost of living that millions of Americans are dealing with.

Trump and his family have long denied any wrongdoing when it comes to their business interests.

And while Miller and Noem did face bipartisan criticism over the administration's crackdown on illegal immigration, the majority of Republicans have lined up behind the White House and maintained that it is what Americans voted for.

Republicans selected House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader in the latest Congress and de facto top spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.
